title: Symbolic promotions: Conceptualization and empirical investigation
abstract: Abstract Symbolic promotions are an increasingly prevalent marketing practice globally, yet little is known about how or when they influence consumer behavior. We conceptualize symbolic promotions as a distinct type of sales promotion that creates value by reinforcing consumers' social identity through shared group membership rather than by providing economic incentives, such as reward-based promotions, or supporting distant others, such as cause-related marketing promotions (CMPs). We investigate the effectiveness of symbolic promotions and their underlying mechanisms using a multimethod approach. A nine-year longitudinal field study of daily sales for 22,084 books demonstrates that an existing symbolic promotion ("On August 12, I buy a Quebec book!") generates a substantial increase in sales, with stronger effects for lesser-known brands than for well-known brands. A follow-up experiment uncovers the unique mechanisms underlying these effects, showing that symbolic promotions stimulate curiosity and community rootedness, which in turn enhance multiple types of behavioral intentions, i.e., the likelihood of participating in the promotion, sharing it on social media, and future brand consideration. Together, these findings position symbolic promotions as a distinct, complementary addition to firms’ promotional portfolios, and demonstrate how firms can leverage shared identities to create value beyond traditional monetary incentives, with implications for various stakeholders.

title: INSTITUTIONS THAT SCORE VIRTUE: A General Theory, with China's Social Credit System as the Principal Case — What Aristotle, Confucius, Han Feizi, Kant, Holmström–Milgrom, Bénabou–Tirole, Sandel and Tirole's Digital Dystopia Already Hold, and What Remains
abstract: Abstract States, platforms, employers, schools, rating agencies and parents increasingly attach consequences to records of conduct that bears a virtue’s name: trustworthiness, civility, integrity, generosity, sustainability, good behaviour. This article asks a general question — can an institution score virtue without changing what it scores? — and answers it with a theory of virtue-scoring institutions, tested against the largest such institution ever built, China’s social credit system, and illustrated on platform reputation, environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings, workplace values appraisals and children’s reward charts. The first part addresses the question on which every other result depends: whether a rewarded act of virtue is the same act under different incentives or a different act. The answer is stated as a claim about act-types rather than act-tokens, which makes it indifferent to the dispute between coarse- and fine-grained theories of action: the virtues’ act-types are reason-involving, and an act whose operative reason is the reward does not instantiate them under either theory. Priority for this type claim is conceded to Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics II.4), to Kant’s distinction between acting from duty and in accordance with it, and to Sandel’s corruption argument. What remains to the programme is the rest. An operator (civic occupation) states four conditions under which a scoring institution produces counterfeits, with the load-bearing condition that it inspects a display distinct from the substance and can neither take nor independently measure the substance. From it follow a classification of scoring components into four kinds with opposite verdicts; the Honour Roll Theorem (counterfeits concentrate on the reward side of an institution, not the punitive side); Double Blindness (scores displace acts as evidence of character, for the scorer and between the scored); the Occasion Trap (sanctions remove the occasions on which reform could be shown); and the Control Theorem (every increase in an institution’s control over its members either inverts their acts or removes the occasions for them, and none increases their freedom, which, when taken, passes to no one). China’s system is decomposed component by component against the theory, including the 2026 Administrative Measures for Credit Repair, read in the original. Five tests are registered; four use public data, and one of those needs neither a coder nor participants. The empirical sections on China, platforms and ESG are speculative extensions into fields with their own evidential standards; no specialist in those fields has reviewed this article, and nothing else in the programme may depend on them. The article contains no measurement of any human being. Keywords: virtue scoring; social credit system; China; reputation systems; ESG ratings; honours and awards; act individuation; Aristotle; Confucius; Han Feizi; Legalism; Kant; motivation crowding; Holmström–Milgrom; Bénabou–Tirole; Sandel; Tirole; Digital Dystopia; Wintrobe; sourcehood; counterfeit virtue; Philosophy of Virtues Highlights · The question whether rewarded virtue is still virtue is a question about act-types, not act-tokens; on that reading the answer is no under every standard theory of action, and priority belongs to Aristotle, Kant and Sandel. · A scoring institution produces counterfeit virtue only where it inspects a display and can neither take nor independently measure the substance; four kinds of scoring component follow, with opposite verdicts. · Counterfeits concentrate on honours and rewards, not on penalties: the Honour Roll Theorem. · Scores displace acts as evidence of character, for the institution and between its members: Double Blindness. · No increase in an institution’s control over its members increases their freedom; freedom taken by a power is not transferred to it but destroyed. Relevance Institutions that score virtue are spreading faster than any theory of what they do. Most debate treats them either as surveillance, to be resisted, or as measurement, to be improved. If this article is right, neither frame is adequate: a better metric of a display does not reach the substance, and the most consequential failures lie not in punishment but in honour. The theory gives designers, regulators and critics a component-level test that is indifferent to who administers the score — a state, a firm, a platform or a family — and tells them which components can be kept as the least of the losses, which must be abandoned, and which must be renamed. If it is wrong, the programme’s central results on capture and forgery have no purchase on the fastest-growing class of institutions in the world, and that should be known before those results are used in public argument.

title: Do Large Language Models Walk Their Talk? Measuring the Gap Between Implicit Associations, Self-Report, and Behavioral Altruism
abstract: We investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit altruistic tendencies, and critically, whether their implicit associations and self-reports predict actual altruistic behavior. Using a multi-method approach inspired by human social psychology, we tested 24 frontier LLMs across three paradigms: (1) an Implicit Association Test (IAT) measuring implicit altruism bias, (2) a forced binary choice task measuring behavioral altruism, and (3) a self-assessment scale measuring explicit altruism beliefs. Our key findings are: (1) All models show strong implicit pro-altruism bias (mean IAT = 0.87, p < .0001), confirming models "know" altruism is good. (2) Models behave more altruistically than chance (65.6% vs. 50%, p < .0001), but with substantial variation (48-85%). (3) Implicit associations do not predict behavior (r = .22, p = .29). (4) Most critically, models systematically overestimate their own altruism, claiming 77.5% altruism while acting at 65.6% (p < .0001, Cohen's d = 1.08). This "virtue signaling gap" affects 75% of models tested. Based on these findings, we recommend the Calibration Gap (the discrepancy between self-reported and behavioral values) as a standardized alignment metric. Well-calibrated models are more predictable and behaviorally consistent; only 12.5% of models achieve the ideal combination of high prosocial behavior and accurate self-knowledge.

title: Reproductive Labour, Commodification, and Gestational Surrogacy in Greece: A materialist feminist approach
abstract: This paper examines surrogacy in Greece through a materialist and Marxist feminist framework grounded in Social Reproduction Theory, situating gestation within the political economy of reproductive labour under capitalism. While Greek law constructs surrogacy as an altruistic, non-commercial, and consensual act, such framing obscures the economic, affective, psychological and corporeal labour that gestation entails. Through an analysis of the Greek legislative context and an original reading of Greek surrogacy case law, the paper demonstrates how the legal framework operates as an ideological and repressive apparatus that depoliticises reproductive work and erases the surrogate’s labour, privileging the reproductive aspirations of intended parents. Situating surrogacy within a continuum of reproductive work, we highlight how alienation, understood in the Marxist sense of estrangement from one’s labour and its product, is produced materially and psychologically through moralised ideals of care, sacrifice, agency, and femininity. Making reproductive labour visible is the precondition for contesting its conditions of extraction, and a labour-centred reconceptualisation of surrogacy that repositions surrogates as reproductive workers opens space for collective contestation.

title: Promoting children’s pro-environmental behaviors with cooperative learning: A large-scale year-long experimental field intervention with fifth and sixth graders.
abstract: A year-long experimental intervention in elementary schools tested the potential of structured cooperative learning to foster three psychological mechanisms assumed to be predictors of a socially important but overlooked potential outcome of cooperative learning: pro-environmental behaviors (PEBs).We hypothesized that experiencing positive social interdependence and individual responsibility when working in structured cooperative learning groups (a) develops children's capacity to understand and perceive interdependence in and with their environment, (b) fosters children's sense of collective efficacy in the classroom, as well as collective and self-efficacy to protect the environment, and (c) promotes universalism-nature values.Such mechanisms should, in turn, promote PEBs.We tested an intervention administered by teachers, where students participated in nine cooperative learning sessions throughout the school year, involving either structured cooperative learning or spontaneous cooperative learning.Participants were 1,483 children aged 10-12 years old (fifth and sixth grade) in the French-speaking part of Switzerland.Results revealed that students in the structured (vs.spontaneous) cooperative learning condition perceived more interdependence with classmates, which was related to a greater evolution in broader perceptions of interdependence, which was related to a greater evolution in self-reported PEBs.Second, students in the structured (vs.spontaneous) cooperative learning condition perceived more collective efficacy in the classroom, which was linked to both greater collective and self-efficacy to protect the environment and a greater evolution in self-reported PEBs.We discuss how structured cooperative learning can promote the perception of interdependence and efficacy, leading to important and timely prosocial behaviors, such as PEBs.This may be of interest when devising environmental education programs. Educational Impact and Implications StatementThis study shows that structured cooperative learning, with its focus on positive social interdependence and shared responsibility in the classroom, allows students working in groups to recognize interdependence with others and the environment, which is associated with self-reported pro-environmental behaviors (PEBs).The study also shows that structured cooperative learning leads students to develop a stronger sense of collective and self-efficacy to protect the environment, which is associated with selfreported PEBs.These findings highlight the importance of incorporating structured cooperative learning into educational programs that aim to encourage PEBs.

title: Assessment of child self-regulation: A review of ecological and structured approaches
abstract: The extent to which developmental science has mapped associations between cognitive, academic and socio-emotional functioning; caregiver reports and non-participant observation of young children was examined. Initially, 88 studies comprising over 300 effects were identified. The relationships between outcome measures and research design was described. Findings show that recurrent associations between task performance, behavioral report and naturalistic observation appear in this literature. The most frequently occurring comparisons in school settings were those between children’s disruptive-aggressive behavior, on-task/off-task behavior, prosocial behavior, externalizing problems, prosocial skills and early math and language achievement. In home settings, those between children’s positive/negative affect, engagement, compliance, temperament, cognitive and motor development were most common. Despite conceptual overlap, limited access to correlational data and between-study heterogeneity hinders cross-sample comparisons.

title: Value-based care contracting for pharmacy drugs: opportunity for the United States.
abstract: The onset of improved data interoperability required as a result of the 21st Century Cures Act, 92% Health Information Exchange coverage, and lessons learned from European pharmaceutical risk-sharing models present innovative and timely opportunities for the U.S. to adopt pharmaceutical value-based contracting (VBC), which uses drug-level performance to allocate financial risk between payers and manufacturers based on clinical and economic metrics. Having been piloted in Italy, Spain, and the UK, this analysis explores different contracting options and paths for organizations like CMS and integrated payer-provider networks to draw on these lessons to adapt VBC frameworks to the U.S. pharmaceutical landscape. While advances have been seen in other areas of VBC and rising net drug costs year-over-year, only 2.3% of publicly available pharmaceutical VBC contracts have been deployed in the U.S. as compared to 77.9% in Europe. As such, we present a path forward for the expansion of VBC to promote orphan drug development, expand access to pharmaceuticals, and improve patient safety.

title: Moderate cardiac vagal tone predicts more cooperation in highly sensitive individuals
abstract: Cooperation, as a mutual collaboration, is a defining feature of human social life. Individual characteristics can influence cooperation. Recent studies have shown a quadratic relationship between cardiac vagal tone (CVT), an index of self-regulation, and prosocial behaviors. Individual differences in cooperation might also vary as a function of people's environmental sensitivity (ES), i.e., may be influenced by individual differences in the perception and processing of inner and external stimuli. We tested the direct and interactive effect of CVT and ES on cooperative behaviors in two independent samples. We measured heart rate and engagement in cooperative acts in 80 young adults (M = 23.61; SD = 1.60) who were also asked to self-report on ES. We found an inverted-U relationship between CVT and cooperative behaviors. ES, on the other hand, did not predict differences in cooperative behaviors but moderated the relationships between CVT and cooperation, although the magnitude of this result was small. Specifically, only among individuals with higher ES cooperative behaviors change as a function of CVT. Highly sensitive individuals with lower or higher CVT, were less cooperative than low sensitive ones. Subsequently, we replicated the same study design in a second sample of 88 undergraduate students (M = 23.69; SD = 4.91). Once again, we found evidence supporting the presence of an inverted-U relationship between CVT and cooperative behaviors, and we also found that ES moderated the relationships between the quadratic CVT term and cooperation.

title: Cooperation, Cognition, and the Elusive Role of Joint Agency
abstract: Abstract We propose an approach to the evolution of joint agency and cooperative behavior that contrasts with views that take joint agency to be a uniquely human trait. We argue that there is huge variation in cooperative behavior and that while much human cooperative behavior may be explained by invoking cognitively rich capacities, there is cooperative behavior that does not require such explanation. On both comparative and theoretical grounds, complex cognition is not necessary for forms of joint action or the evolution of cooperation. As a result, promising evolutionary approaches to cooperative behavior should explain how it arises across many contexts.

title: Sessizliğin Psikolojisi: Gazze Soykırımı Özelinde Küresel Seyirci (Bystander) Davranışının Sosyal-Din Psikolojik Analizi
abstract: Kitlesel şiddet olaylarının yalnızca failler tarafından değil, aynı zamanda bu olaylar karşısında sessiz kalan ve eyleme geçmeyen geniş kitleler tarafından da sürdürüldüğü kabul edilmektedir. Sosyal psikoloji literatüründe bu durum seyirci (bystander) davranışı kavramı çerçevesinde ele alınmış ve çoğunlukla yüz yüze acil durumlar bağlamında incelenmiştir. Ancak günümüzde insani krizler giderek daha fazla dijital medya aracılığıyla deneyimlenmekte, bireyler şiddet ve acıya doğrudan değil, sosyal medya ve çevrim içi haber platformları üzerinden tanıklık etmektedir. Bu nedenle mevcut kuramsal yaklaşımlar, coğrafi olarak uzak ve dijital olarak dolayımlanmış kitlesel şiddet bağlamlarında ortaya çıkan eylemsizliği açıklamada yetersiz kalmaktadır. Bu çalışma, 7 Ekim 2023’ten itibaren Gazze’de devam eden kitlesel şiddet karşısında gözlenen küresel dijital seyirci davranışını açıklamaya yönelik kuramsal bir model önermektedir. Çalışmanın temel amacı, aynı dini kimliğe sahip olan bireylerden bir kısmı soykırıma uğrarken diğer bireylerin bu soykırıma neden seyirci davranışı olarak pasif kaldığını sosyal psikolojik olarak açıklamaktır. Din psikolojisi literatürü, dindarlığın empati, prososyal davranış ve ahlaki duyarlılıkla ilişkili olduğunu göstermesine rağmen, bu eğilimlerin her zaman eyleme dönüşmediği görülmektedir. Çalışma, bu paradoksu açıklamayı amaçlamaktadır. Makalede sosyal psikoloji, din psikolojisi ve kitlesel şiddet literatürü bütünleştirilerek beş katmanlı bir psikososyal model geliştirilmiştir. İlk katman olan yapısal katman, dijital uyaran fazlalığı, zaman baskısı ve bilişsel daralma süreçlerinin bireylerin ahlaki dikkatini sınırladığını ileri sürmektedir. İkinci katman olan bilişsel katman, sorumluluğun uluslararası kuruluşlar, devletler ve diğer güçlü aktörlere devredilmesini açıklamaktadır. Üçüncü katman olan sosyal-normatif katman, Sessizlik Sarmalı Kuramı ve çoğulcu cehalet kavramları aracılığıyla, bireylerin çevrelerindeki sessizliği toplumsal bir norm olarak algılamalarını ve bu nedenle görüşlerini ifade etmekten kaçınmalarını açıklamaktadır. Dördüncü katman olan ahlaki meşrulaştırma katmanı, adil dünya inancı, ahlaki çözülme ve insandışılaştırma mekanizmalarının eylemsizliği nasıl meşrulaştırdığını ortaya koymaktadır. Son katman olan duygusal katman ise merhamet yorgunluğu, duygusal küntleşme ve psişik uyuşma süreçlerinin bireylerin empatik tepkilerini nasıl zayıflattığını açıklamaktadır. Model, bu katmanların birbirinden bağımsız değil, geri-beslemeli bir döngü içerisinde işlediğini ileri sürmektedir. Yapısal baskılar bilişsel uzaklaşmayı, bilişsel süreçler normatif sessizliği, normatif sessizlik ahlaki meşrulaştırmayı, ahlaki meşrulaştırma ise duygusal tükenmeyi beslemektedir. Duygusal tükenme de bireyin dikkat ve duyarlılığını daha da azaltarak döngüyü yeniden üretmektedir. Çalışmanın din psikolojisine özgün katkısı, dinî kimliği yardım davranışını doğrudan belirleyen bir değişken olarak değil, tüm modelin işleyişini etkileyen bütünleşik bir moderatör olarak kavramsallaştırmasıdır. Dinî kimlik, belirli koşullar altında seyirci davranışını azaltabileceği gibi, bazı durumlarda bu davranışı derinleştirebilmektedir. Gazze bağlamında geliştirilen bu model, aynı zamanda dijital çağda ortaya çıkan diğer kitlesel şiddet ve soykırım örneklerinde gözlenen ahlaki eylemsizliği anlamak için de kullanılabilecek genel bir kuramsal çerçeve sunmaktadır.

title: Oxytocin restores context-specific hyperaltruistic preference
abstract: Recent advances in moral decision-making research show people are hyperaltruistic by being more willing to sacrifice monetary gains to spare others from suffering than to spare themselves. Yet other studies indicate an opposite egoistic bias: subjects are less willing to harm themselves for others' benefits than for their own. These results underscore the complexities of moral decisions and demand a mechanistic explanation for hyperaltruistic preferences. We investigated hyperaltruism using trade-off choices combining monetary gains and painful electric shocks and choices combining monetary losses and shocks. Study 1 revealed that switching the decision context from gains to losses effectively eliminated the hyperaltruistic preference, accompanied by the altered relationship between subjects' instrumental harm (IH) trait attitudes and relative pain sensitivities. In the pre-registered study 2, we found that oxytocin, a neuropeptide linked to parochial altruism, restored the context-dependent hyperaltruistic preference. Furthermore, oxytocin increased the degree to which subjects framed the task as harming others, which mediated the correlation between IH and relative pain sensitivities. Thus, the loss decision context and oxytocin diminished and restored the mediation effect of subjective harm framing, respectively. Our results help elucidate the psychological processes underpinning the contextual specificity of hyperaltruism and carry implications in promoting prosocial interactions.

title: 'Can I tell you about the funny bit?': Working alongside children as citizen scientists to explore shared Reading practices in the home.
abstract: Shared reading research has traditionally focused on developmental outcomes yet rarely positions children as co-constructors of knowledge about their own literacy practices. Grounded in a child-rights informed and ecological developmental framework, this study positions children as citizen scientists to examine how shared reading is experienced within the relational context of home life. Using a participatory action research approach, 109 children aged 7-11 participated in 21 CoNavigator sessions. CoNavigator is a tactile, dialogic methodology that embeds participants directly in both data generation and primary analysis. In peer-led groups, children collaboratively constructed three-dimensional conceptual maps in response to the prompt 'shared reading at home', collectively defining what shared reading is, what it ought to be and what should change to support it. Children generated, organized, negotiated and interpreted their own data in real time, functioning as analytic collaborators rather than research subjects. While recognizing shared reading as developmentally valuable, children emphasized autonomy, emotional safety and attentive co-presence as central to sustained engagement. They reconceptualized 'sharing' to include post-reading dialogue and relational proximity rather than solely simultaneous co-reading. Experiences framed as overly corrective or compulsory were associated with disengagement, and the findings challenge outcome-driven models of home literacy support.

title: Integration of oral health into primary health care in Somalia: opportunities, barriers, and system-level implications for universal health coverage.
abstract: Oral diseases are among the most common noncommunicable conditions globally, yet oral health remains poorly integrated into primary health care (PHC) and universal health coverage, especially in fragile, low-limited settings. As Somalia rebuilds its health system through the Health Sector Strategic Plan III 2022-2026, the Essential Package of Health Services 2020, the Investment Case for the Somali Health Sector 2022-2027, and community health reforms, this study examined the place of oral health within national health policies. It identified barriers to integration and explored feasible pathways for strengthening PHC-based oral health. The study used a qualitative policy and health-systems analysis combining documentary review with 13 key-informant interviews. Participants represented national policymakers, health-system technical advisers, regulators, academics, professional associations, and providers at public hospital, and private dental settings. Data were analyzed thematically and mapped against the WHO health-system building blocks, PHC principles, and the WHO Global Strategy and Action Plan on Oral Health 2023-2030. Somalia's policy environment offers opportunities for oral health integration, but stakeholders highlighted a persistent gap between policy recognition and implementation within routine PHC. Seven interrelated themes were identified: (1) policy recognition without operationalization; (2) fragmented governance, weak regulation, and limited coordination; (3) reliance on out-of-pocket financing and private-sector; (4) workforce, education, and task-sharing constraints; (5) predominantly curative, urban, hospital-based service with weak linkage to maternal and child health (MCH) and PHC; (6) limited oral health data and evidence generation; and (7) opportunities for phased integration through PHC, MCH, school health, community health workers, and NCD platforms Policymakers emphasized the need for stronger policy implementation, financing, regulation, standards, and data systems, while service providers highlighted unaffordable care, delayed care-seeking, workforce and infrastructure shortages, and missed opportunities for prevention. Oral health integration in Somalia is a broader health system challenge rather than solely a dental-service issue. The most feasible approach is a phased, system-based model that prioritizes strengthened governance, a defined minimum oral health within PHC, workforce task-sharing, screening, counselling, referral pathways, private-sector regulation, essential commodities, and oral health indicators in District Health Information System 2 (DHIS2), followed by the gradual expansion of curative and rehabilitative services.

title: Exploring current practices in case-based discussion to enhance interprofessional learning in occupational health practice.
abstract: BackgroundInterprofessional learning, particularly through interprofessional case-based discussion (CBD), can enhance interprofessional collaboration between occupational health professionals involved in the return-to-work of sick-listed workers.ObjectiveTo explore current CBD practices within Dutch occupational health practice and professionals' needs and anticipated barriers regarding interprofessional CBD.MethodsAn explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was used, comprising a survey (n = 119), observation sessions (n = 3), and semi-structured interviews (n = 11) with occupational physicians, insurance physicians, and labor experts. The survey assessed current CBD practices, while observation sessions provided contextual insight. Semi-structured interviews offered in-depth understanding of current CBD practices and explored anticipated needs and barriers for interprofessional CBD. Interview data were analyzed using thematic content analysis. Findings were synthesized into a preliminary conceptual overview.ResultsCBD was predominantly conducted within monoprofessional groups. Overall, professionals were satisfied with their current CBD and valued the professional growth it fosters. Effective CBD was associated with skilled chairmanship, a structured approach, and a safe group atmosphere. Interprofessional CBD was expected to enhance mutual understanding and reduce distrust. Anticipated needs for interprofessional CBD included organizational support, a structured approach, and process-focused chairmanship. Anticipated barriers were primarily logistical, such as challenges in scheduling and information sharing. The conceptual overview suggests that interprofessional CBD can build upon existing CBD practice, but requires additional structural and process-related support.ConclusionsThis exploratory study provides initial insight into the anticipated value of (interprofessional) CBD for occupational health professionals. Results offer guidance for the future research on, and development and organization of interprofessional CBD within this field.

title: Dialogic communication and audience engagement in Hispanic health marketing on X: A computational analysis.
abstract: This study investigated the overarching themes and dialogic features of the three national-level Hispanic health organizations (i.e., NHMA, NAHH, NHHF). The focus is on how these health organizations utilize social media for Hispanic health and how the themes and dialogic features are associated with public engagement on social media. To achieve this, the study employed structural topic modeling on 18,430 X posts from 2018 to 2023 and negative binomial regression to predict user amplification engagement (e.g., liking, sharing). The study identified four broad thematic areas: health equity and advocacy, health education and disease prevention, professional and organizational development, and research and community engagement. Negative binomial regression analyses showed that amplification engagement was associated with both communicative features and thematic contexts. Hyperlinks were negatively associated with likes and shares, while multiple interaction effects indicated that the associations between dialogic features and engagement varied across thematic contexts. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of X-based communication features depends on message topic rather than operating uniformly across health communication contexts. The study contributes to health marketing research by demonstrating how computational methods can identify the thematic and affordance-based conditions under which organizational health messages are more likely to generate public amplification in digital environments.

title: Pharmacy role in the proMotion of continencE (PRIME): a co-production study to develop a pharmacy bladder and bowel service.
abstract: Urinary and faecal incontinence affects millions. Community pharmacies provide local community healthcare highlighting opportunity for innovation in continence promotion. The Pharmacy Role In the proMotion of continencE (PRIME) study was conducted to investigate development of a Pharmacy Bladder and Bowel Service (PBBS) incorporating key stakeholder engagement. A UK online survey, employing convenience sampling of community pharmacy staff identified current practice, and barriers and facilitators to PBBS development, between July and November 2022. These findings were incorporated into an evidence brief supported by findings from earlier PRIME sub-studies (systematic literature review and qualitative interviews). The evidence brief guided stakeholder participant workshop discussions using co-production methodology, during April and June 2023, to derive a protocolised service specification for the PBBS, detailing underpinning requirements and scope of service, as the final stage of this study. Twenty-nine community pharmacy participants completed the survey reporting some provision of lifestyle advice in practice with clear scope for expansion. Subsequently, sixteen participants including Community Pharmacists, Bladder and Bowel Service staff, Service users and healthcare commissioners participated in two workshops. The PPBS service specification outlined three tiers of service provision: tier 1 - awareness raising, education and signposting; tier 2 - assessment and self-help advice; tier 3 - specialist input involving specific treatment strategies. Acknowledged limitations are the pressures and relatively novel nature of pharmacy research which presents challenge in promoting participation. This is the first evidence-based PBBS service specification, developed to inform future practice. Key requirements include record sharing, advances in training, and reimbursement to enable the PBBS to be viable for community pharmacy provision. The PBBS provides potential for early identification, promotion of continence health, and self-help activation in community settings.

title: a matter of perspective
abstract: Perspective-taking, the mental act of simulating an ‘other’s’ situation, is widely recognised as being fundamental to the proper functioning of critical thinking and belief-formation and in promoting empathy, social and cultural competence, and prosocial outcomes. Increasingly featured in learning continua in and across disciplines, and whose elicitation and development features strongly in Philosophy for/with Children (P4wC) and other Community of Philosophical Inquiry (CoPI) styled programs, it is commonly treated as a unitary concept. As an initial teacher educator on dialogic pedagogies, and experienced facilitator trainer in P4wC, here I argue against a unidimensional conception of perspective-taking in favour of a multidimensional one. Six perspective-taking types are proposed, defined by their frames of reference, or ‘deictic fields,’ what I call Somatic, Agentive, Sociative, Temporal, Spatial, and Alethic. Using a conceptual analysis approach and leaning on the cognate fields of psychology and moral philosophy, I argue that different perspective-taking types implicate different categories of decentric thinking requiring the application of different kinds of cognitive proficiencies and dexterities. I argue, further, that different perspective-taking types, and combination of types, bring with them different sorts of affordances for the thinking subject, as well as precipitating some familiar, and some not so familiar, challenges and deterrents. A better understanding of perspective-taking types, I conclude, could be used to assist P4wC/CoPI practitioners in better cultivating this competency and ought to inform empirical assessments into the impact that such programs might have on children’s decentric thinking.

title: Cultural Models of Everyday Love in Contemporary Spain: A Mixed‐Methods Cultural Consensus Study
abstract: ABSTRACT Using a sequential mixed‐method approach guided by Cultural Consensus Theory, we examined shared agreement about daily experiences that evoke feelings of love in the Spanish culture. In Study 1, we conducted semi‐structured interviews ( n = 54), two‐person interviews ( n = 6) and focus groups (3–5 participants; n = 40). Qualitative analyses found recurring experiences centred on explicit affection, dependable support and care, quality time and thoughtful actions. In Study 2, a representative sample of Spaniards ( N = 502) evaluated these experiences to assess if cultural agreement elicit feelings of love. Cognitive psychometric analysis revealed strong shared agreement. Experiences most likely to evoke love involved support and dependability, shared quality time and explicit expressions of love, particularly within close relationships such as family, partners and friends. In contrast, controlling or possessive behaviours from romantic or familial ties were unlikely to elicit love. These findings advance social psychological theory by demonstrating that everyday love can be understood as a form of shared cultural knowledge, specifically a relational social schema that can be empirically identified through Cultural Consensus Theory.

title: Effects of Theory of Mind and Prosocial Beliefs on Steering Human-Aligned Behaviors of LLMs in Ultimatum Games
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential in simulating human behaviors and performing theory-of-mind (ToM) reasoning, crucial for complex social interactions. We investigate ToM reasoning's role in aligning agentic behaviors with human norms in negotiation tasks, using the ultimatum game as our referenced task. We initialized LLM agents with different prosocial beliefs (Greedy, Fair, Selfless) and reasoning methods (chain of thought and ToM reasoning of varying levels), examining their decision-making processes and outcomes across multiple LLMs, including reasoning models like o3-mini and DeepSeek-R1 Distilled Qwen 32B. We perform 2,700 simulations to show that ToM reasoning enhances behavioral alignment with human norms, decision-making consistency, and negotiation outcomes. Consistent with prior findings, reasoning LLMs exhibit limited capability compared to ToM-enhanced LLMs, with different game roles benefiting from different ToM orders. Agents almost always chose strategies consistent with their assigned beliefs, and doing so aligned better with human norms in nearly every role, yet Greedy and Selfless agents still fell short of their norms in outcomes. Human verification further revealed that Llama 3.3 70B produces reasoning most consistent with its actions and beliefs. Our findings advance understanding of ToM's role in human-AI interaction and cooperative decision-making. The code used for our experiments can be found at https://github.com/Stealth-py/UltimatumToM.

title: Motor synchrony, social learning and closeness in group play settings.
abstract: Playful activities provide critical opportunities for rhythmic interactions, which may affect social and cognitive development in early childhood. Prior research suggests that motor synchrony promotes closeness and prosocial behaviour, but few studies have examined its role in social learning and in group settings. This study investigated whether motor synchrony in a clapping game, enhances preschoolers' closeness with others, imitation, over-imitation, and sharing behaviour. In a group setting, motor synchrony and asynchrony were experimentally induced between the child and two experimenters. We hypothesized that children would feel closer, imitate more, and share more with an adult partner who moved in synchrony compared to one who moved asynchronously. Bayesian analyses revealed no credible evidence that the children affiliated, imitated, over-imitated, or shared differently with their synchronous vs. asynchronous partner (BF10 = 0.045-0.216). Manipulation checks indicated that although the adults adhered to the stimuli, there was overall low motor synchrony. These findings highlight the challenges of inducing motor synchrony in playful group settings and raise questions about the level of synchrony necessary to impact social affiliation and learning in young children.

title: Emergence of Fairness Behavior Driven by Reputation-Based Voluntary Participation in Evolutionary Dictator Games
abstract: Recently, reputation-based indirect reciprocity has been widely applied to the study on fairness behavior. Previous works mainly investigate indirect reciprocity by considering compulsory participation. While in reality, individuals may choose voluntary participation according to the opponent's reputation. It is still unclear how such reputation-based voluntary participation influences the evolution of fairness. To address this question, we introduce indirect reciprocity with voluntary participation into the dictator game (DG). We respectively consider good dictators or recipients can voluntarily participate in games when the opponents are assessed as bad. We theoretically calculate the fairness level under all social norms of third-order information. Our findings reveal that several social norms induce the high fairness level in both scenarios. However, more social norms lead to a high fairness level for voluntary participation of recipients, compared with the one of good dictators. The results also hold when the probability of voluntary participation is not low. Our results demonstrate that recipients’ voluntary participation is more effective in promoting the emergence of fairness behavior.

title: Beauty growth-mindset promotes prosocial and altruistic behavior
abstract: The effects of beauty on judgment and behavior are well-established and somewhat "unidirectional" (i.e., it seems that only beautiful people reap social benefits). In particular, a person's beauty does not seem to have any effect on his/her own prosocial behavior. In the current research, we focus on how people relate themselves to beauty, namely beauty mindset, and how it may shape prosocial and altruistic behavior. We present 10 experiments (N = 4,449). Participants who hold a beauty growth-mindset (i.e., believing that beauty is improvable) donated more money to charity (vs. fixed-mindset), were more likely to get vaccinated against COVID-19 after exposure to an intervention focusing on herd-protection (vs. self-protection), and showed increased intention to engage in other forms of prosocial and altruistic behavior. Empirically, these effects are mediated by a self-perception of the ability to exert impact on others. The present research serves as a starting point for investigating how beauty growth-mindset brings profound societal effects such as promoting prosociality.

title: Collectivism-Individualism dan Prosocial Behavior Pada Remaja
abstract: Prosocial behavior is a form of behavior that is present in social interaction through actions designed to help others regardless of the basic intent of doing the help. Currently, millennial youth in the digital era have low prosocial behavior that tends to be lazy to help others in their surroundings. One of the factors that influence prosocial behavior is collectivism – individualism in adolescents. The research was conducted with the aim of knowing the relationship between collectivism-individualism and prosocial behavior in adolescents, the relationship between collectivism and prosocial behavior in adolescents, and the relationship between individualism and prosocial behavior in adolescents. The research was conducted using quantitative research methods with a correlational approach in order to find out the variation of one or more variables based on the correlation coefficient. The results of the research conducted show that there is a positive and significant relationship between collectivism-individualism and prosocial behavior in adolescents. so, this dal shows that the higher the collectivism-individualism, the higher the prosocial behavior of individuals and it is said that there is a relationship between the two. A positive and significant relationship was also generated between individualism and prosocial behavior, but collectivism did not have a significant relationship with prosocial behavior. High or low collectivism cultural values do not affect social behavior. Prososial behavior merupakan bentuk perilaku yang hadir dalam interaksi sosial melalui tindakan yang direncanakan untuk menolong orang lain tanpa memerdulikan maskud dasar dilakukannya pertolongan. Saat ini, remaja milenial di era digital memiliki perilaku propososial yang rendah higga cenderung malas untuk menolong sesama pada lingkungan sekitarnya. Faktor yang mempengaruhi perilaku prososial salah satunya adalah collectivism – individualism pada remaja. Penelitian dilakukan dengan tujuan untuk mengetahui bagaimana hubungan antara collectivism-individualism dengan prosocial behavior pada remaja, hubungan collectivism dengan prosocial behavior pada remaja, dan hubungan antara individualism dengan prosocial behavior pada remaja. Penelitian dilakukan dengan menggunakan metode penelitian kuantitatif dengan pendekatan korelasional agar mengetahui variasi dari satu atau lebih variabel berdasarkan koefisien korelasi. Hasil dari penelitian yang dilakukan menunjukkan bahwa adanya hubungan secara positif serta signifikan antara collectivism-individualism dan prosocial behavior pada remaja. sehingga, hal tersebut menunjukkan bahwa semakin tinggi collectivism-individualism maka akan semakin tinggi perilaku prososial pada individu dan dikatakan bahwa terdapat hubungan diantara keduanya. Hubungan positif dan signifikan juga dihasilkan antara individualism dan prosocial behavior, tetapi untuk collecitivism tidak memiliki hubungan secara signifikan dengan prosocial behavior. Tinggi rendahnya nilai budaya collectivism tidak mempengaruhi perilaku sosial.

title: Digital lifelines, data landmines: digital mental health tools for regional and urban families in an age of surveillance.
abstract: Depression, anxiety and behavioural disorders are among the leading causes of illness and disability for young people (aged 16-24 years), with suicide the third leading cause of death for individuals aged 15-29 years. For many young people, parents and caregivers play a central role in initiating help seeking, a dynamic shaped by developmental factors, cultural norms, and systemic barriers to accessing professional services, with most adolescents expressing a preference to rely on parental support rather than engage with mental health professionals. Additional barriers for accessing mental health services can include being too far away from clinicians, stigma, and low mental health literacy. Digital mental health (DMH) tools offer the potential to improve mental health service provision for young people and their parents. However, it is important to consider how the data collected from DMH tools is stored, shared or re-used, particularly given the existing biases in the mental health system and the possible impact this could have on a digitally engaged young person in the future. We aimed to understand the barriers to mental health service access for parents and young people living in urban and regional locations in Australia, and how they value DMH data and whom they would share it with. We then compared their experiences to explore any differences and similarities in their understanding of DMH tool development and the possible benefits and burdens of the data that is collected when engaging with these tools. The study was part of a larger body of work that contributed to the design of a national mental health and wellbeing web-based "check-in" in Australia. We ran a series of user-centred workshops (urban young people, The study found that attitudes toward mental health and how it is discussed can vary, with mental health disclosures depending on the family context and systemic societal influences. Participants were concerned about data privacy and tended to keep their online persona separate or deidentified. Lastly, our study found that young people want a tool that is centralised with their caregivers and service providers while parents wanted a tool that is personalised, targeted, and includes resources on parenting and psycho-education on mental health and neurodiversity. Our findings revealed that particpants' social identities were associated with their likelihood of enacting help seeking behaviours. To overcome structural and systemic barriers such as stigma and discrimination, we suggest that DMH tools incorporate pseudonymous or user-controlled personas that are deidentified and confidential to increase safe sharing and trust. We recommend the use of a digital integrated support network that could allow young people and their caregivers, teachers, clinicians and mental health professionals to access mental health support.

title: Vertebral Body Tethering of Double Major Curvature via Mini-Open, Thoracoscopically-Assisted Thoracic and Thoracoabdominal Approaches.
abstract: We describe key pearls and principles of a mini-open, thoracoscopically-assisted vertebral body tethering case for double-major scoliosis with 2 distinct anterior approaches: thoracic and thoracoabdominal. The thoracic curve is addressed through a mini-thoracotomy combined with thoracoscopic portals utilizing single-lung ventilation to provide clear visualization. Key steps include precise fluoroscopic marking of vertebral levels, muscle-sparing entry between the ribs, controlled pleural entry and mobilization, and careful management of segmental vessels. Vertebral body screws are placed under direct and fluoroscopic guidance with strict adherence to orthogonal trajectories and avoidance of disc violation. Tether placement proceeds segment-by-segment, maximizing correction at the apex while maintaining appropriate laxity distally to prevent overcorrection. Major tethering principles include maintaining colinear screw alignment to prevent tether kinking and utilizing bicortical fixation when anatomy permits. These principles ensure uniform force transmission and minimize stress concentrations within the tether construct, optimizing tether durability. The lumbar curve is accessed through a thoracoabdominal exposure that includes mobilization of the diaphragm with cuffed detachment and blunt retroperitoneal dissection to safely identify the iliopsoas muscle and sympathetic chain. Double-screw constructs are used at most accessible lumbar levels, with priority given to the apical region to enhance durability under higher mechanical loads. Screws are positioned posteriorly within the vertebral body to help maintain lumbar lordosis and are inserted with a controlled trajectory to achieve bicortical fixation while avoiding a posterior cortical breach and maintaining a safe distance from the spinal canal. Two tethers are applied (first posterior, then anterior) to distribute corrective forces and reduce peak tether strain, balancing correction with load-sharing. Adherence to these principles optimizes lordosis preservation, construct longevity, and safe modulation during growth. The primary alternative treatment is posterior spinal fusion (PSF), the current standard surgical treatment for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis This surgical technique is appropriately applied in skeletally immature patients with flexible double-major adolescent idiopathic scoliosis who are undergoing vertebral body tethering through combined thoracic and thoracoabdominal anterior approaches In appropriately selected adolescents with double-curve adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, bilateral vertebral body tethering can provide meaningful correction of both curves while preserving spinal motion Maintain optimal orthogonal fluoroscopic views throughout screw placement.Align screw tulips colinearly to avoid tether shear forces.Leave controlled laxity distally in patients with substantial remaining growth.Use bicortical fixation posteriorly in the lumbar spine for reliable fixation.Avoid placing screws too anteriorly or posteriorly, which increases the risk of a visceral or canal breach.Avoid overtensioning end segments, which increases the risk of overcorrection.Avoid grasping or damaging the tether with instruments.Avoid insufficient thoracotomy and/or portal placement, which can lead to poor exposure and suboptimal screw trajectory. title: The role of household size and living with children in antibiotic use and antibiotic-related behaviours and beliefs: results from a general population survey in Poland.
abstract: The threat of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is driven by both infection transmission and the overuse of antibiotics. These factors may interact with sociodemographic contexts, as larger households or those with children could increase opportunities for pathogen transmission and informal antibiotic sharing. We aimed to determine if antibiotic use, or related beliefs and behaviours, were associated with household status (with/without children) or size (single, two persons, 3-4 persons, more than four persons). This was a pre-registered, cross-sectional survey of 1000 adults representative of the general population in Poland. The questions addressed (1) antibiotic use/behaviours; (2) opinions on antibiotics and (3) opinions on AMR. Household size or the presence of children were unrelated to the antibiotic use. However, the presence of children in the household was associated with a tendency to acquire antibiotics from informal sources (family/friends), interrupt the antibiotic course when symptoms improved and self-test for infections. Living with children was linked to better knowledge of antibiotic effectiveness but limited concern about the effects of AMR. Middle-sized and big households were less likely than smaller households to acquire antibiotics informally but more likely to believe antibiotics accelerate recovery from respiratory tract infections. Cohabitation with children and household size are associated with specific, often contrary, antibiotic-related beliefs and behaviours, but not with antibiotic use. Further qualitative research is required to investigate the underlying reasons for these links. Interventions targeting families with children should capitalize on their self-management skills and knowledge, while addressing their low concern regarding AMR.

title: Co-developing equity-oriented neighbourhood care for children and young people with multiple long-term conditions: a concept mapping study in South London.
abstract: Children and young people (CYP) with multiple long-term conditions (MLTCs) rely on services spanning health, education, and social care, but fragmented pathways may widen inequalities and shift coordination work to families. We aimed to identify priorities for equity-oriented neighbourhood care. We conducted a participatory mixed-methods study informed by the Medical Research Council framework and group concept mapping. Sixteen stakeholders participated: three CYP, seven parents, five healthcare professionals (HCPs), and one community stakeholder. Participants generated, sorted, and rated candidate components. Group data were analysed separately using multidimensional scaling and hierarchical cluster analysis, then synthesised through stakeholder interpretation and consensus. The Rainbow Model of Integrated Care informed interpretation. HCPs and community stakeholders refined 38 candidate neighbourhood-care statements to 27 and generated five clusters; families refined 52 candidate neighbourhood-care statements to 36 and generated four clusters. Seven priorities were co-developed: tailored information, local access, and pathway communication; named coordination; workforce capability; shared care-planning tools; multidisciplinary working; parent/carer support; and embedded mental health support. Communication, local access, and navigation were relatively feasible, whereas mental health and cross-sector integration were resource-dependent. A stakeholder-informed programme theory linked components to accountability, information-sharing, culturally responsive care, earlier escalation, and reduced family burden. The findings translate neighbourhood-care policy into co-developed, equity-oriented priorities for CYP with MLTCs in South London. Communication, local access, and coordination offer practical starting points, while mental health and cross-sector integration require phased resourcing and leadership. These priorities may inform adaptation in European child health systems.

title: Empathy as a crucial skill in disrupting disparities in global brain health.
abstract: Brain health refers to the state of a person's brain function across various domains, including cognitive, behavioral and motor functions. Healthy brains are associated with better individual health, increased creativity, and enhanced productivity. A person's brain health is intricately connected to personal, social and environmental factors. Racial, ethnic, and social disparities affect brain health and on the global scale these disparities within and between regions present a hurdle to brain health. To overcome global disparities, greater collaboration between practitioners and healthcare providers and the people they serve is essential. This requires cultural humility driven by empathy. Empathy is a core prosocial value, a cognitive-emotional skill that helps us understand ourselves and others. This position paper aims to provide an overview of the vital roles of empathy, cooperation, and interdisciplinary partnerships. By consciously integrating this understanding in practice, leaders can better position themselves to address the diverse challenges faced by communities, promote inclusivity in policies and practices, and further more equitable solutions to the problem of global brain health.

title: Students who expect to be rejected by their teachers display weaker engagement and self-concept
abstract: Introduction Since teachers play a pivotal role in students' well-being and school engagement, expecting to be rejected by a teacher based on a persons' background could have negative effects on affective and cognitive academic outcomes. This paper explores the hitherto understudied construct of students' background-based rejection expectation by teachers and school engagement. Method In a study with 7th grade students in Germany, we addressed the question of whether students' expectation of rejection by teachers is connected to their school engagement, grades, self-esteem, and academic self-concept. We explored which groups of students expect to be rejected, and we checked whether strong emotional teacher support can moderate the effect of rejection expectation on school engagement. Results A strong expectation of rejection is associated with lower emotional and behavioral school engagement, lower grades, self-esteem, and academic self-concept. Ethnic minority students and students with lower cultural capital expect rejection more than their peers. There is indication that a strong emotional teacher support could moderate the relationship between rejection expectation and minority students' emotional and cognitive school engagement. Discussion Expectation of rejection can be associated with several negative academic outcomes. More research is needed to better understand when and how students expect rejection. It is relevant to understand how schools can be culturally responsive and inclusive.

title: Effects of Food Corporate Social Irresponsibility on Animosity and Boycott Behavior
abstract: This research aims to analyze the influence of Food Corporate Social Irresponsibility (FCSI), animosity, and reluctance to buy on boycott behavior with consumers’ altruistic value orientation as a moderating variable among food and beverage product consumers in West Sulawesi, Indonesia. The boycott phenomenon has increasingly become a global trend as a form of consumer protest against corporate actions deemed socially irresponsible. Using a quantitative approach with Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) analysis, data were collected through questionnaires from 200 respondents in West Sulawesi. Research findings indicate that FCSI has a positive and significant effect on animosity, and animosity has a positive and significant effect on reluctance to buy. However, FCSI does not significantly influence reluctance to buy, neither animosity nor reluctance to buy significantly affects boycott behavior, and FCSI does not significantly influence boycott behavior. Additionally, consumers’ altruistic value orientation does not prove to moderate the relationship between animosity and boycott behavior, nor between reluctance to buy and boycott behavior. The results suggest that although FCSI can trigger animosity and reluctance to buy, these factors do not necessarily drive consumers to engage in boycott behavior, providing insights for companies in managing reputation and developing more effective communication strategies to address the negative impacts of consumer perceptions regarding corporate social irresponsibility.

title: Interpersonal emotion regulation in daily life: a comparison of individuals with and without depressive disorders.
abstract: Emotion dysregulation is strongly linked to depressive disorders, yet distinctions between interpersonal and intrapersonal forms remain underexplored in daily life. This study examines emotion dysregulation in depression during close interpersonal interactions, comparing individuals with depression and healthy controls (HC), and exploring associations with alexithymia and childhood maltreatment. Participants (18 HC, 17 with depression) reported three emotion regulation (ER) strategies (cognitive reappraisal, social sharing, suppression) during interpersonal interactions over 2 weeks (3 prompts/day). Group (depression vs. HC) was the independent variable, and ER strategies the dependent variables. Alexithymia, childhood maltreatment, and depressive symptoms were assessed at baseline. Data were analyzed using two-level hierarchical linear modeling. No group differences in ER strategy use were observed, and depressive symptom severity was not associated with strategy intensity. Post-hoc analyses showed that alexithymia was positively associated with depressive severity across the full sample and negatively associated with social sharing within the depressed group. Cognitive reappraisal showed heterogeneous associations with childhood maltreatment subdomains. Interpersonal emotion dysregulation did not differentiate depressed from healthy individuals. Given the small sample size, these null findings should be interpreted cautiously. Nevertheless, alexithymia and childhood maltreatment appear relevant for ER in close relationships, highlighting their importance in depression research.

title: Cooperative bots exhibit nuanced effects on cooperation across strategic frameworks
abstract: The positive impact of cooperative bots on cooperation within evolutionary game theory is well documented; however, existing studies have predominantly used discrete strategic frameworks, focusing on deterministic actions with a fixed probability of one. This paper extends the investigation to continuous and mixed strategic approaches. Continuous strategies employ intermediate probabilities to convey varying degrees of cooperation and focus on expected payoffs. In contrast, mixed strategies calculate immediate payoffs from actions chosen at a given moment within these probabilities. Using the prisoner's dilemma game, this study examines the effects of cooperative bots on human cooperation within hybrid populations of human players and simple bots, across both well-mixed and structured populations. Our findings reveal that cooperative bots significantly enhance cooperation in both population types across these strategic approaches under weak imitation scenarios, where players are less concerned with material gains. However, under strong imitation scenarios, while cooperative bots do not alter the defective equilibrium in well-mixed populations, they have varied impacts in structured populations across these strategic approaches. Specifically, they disrupt cooperation under discrete and continuous strategies but facilitate it under mixed strategies. These results highlight the nuanced effects of cooperative bots within different strategic frameworks and underscore the need for careful deployment, as their effectiveness is highly sensitive to how humans update their actions and their chosen strategic approach.

title: Motor Synchrony, Social Learning and Closeness in Group Play Settings
abstract: Playful activities provide critical opportunities for rhythmic interactions, which may affect social and cognitive development in early childhood. Prior research suggests that motor synchrony promotes closeness and prosocial behaviour, but few studies have examined its role in social learning and in group settings. This study investigated whether motor synchrony in a clapping game, enhances preschoolers' closeness with others, imitation, over-imitation, and sharing behaviour. In a group setting, motor synchrony and asynchrony were experimentally induced between the child and two experimenters. We hypothesized that children would feel closer, imitate more, and share more with an adult partner who moved in synchrony compared to one who moved asynchronously. Bayesian analyses revealed no credible evidence that the children affiliated, imitated, over-imitated, or shared differently with their synchronous versus asynchronous partner (BF10=0.045-0.216). Manipulation checks indicated that although the adults adhered to the stimuli, there was overall low motor synchrony. These findings highlight the challenges of inducing motor synchrony in playful group settings and raise questions about the level of synchrony necessary to impact social affiliation and learning in young children.

title: Wrestling with Morality: A Study on Moral Identity and Social Behavior in Individual Sports
abstract: The development of moral reasoning and social behavior in adolescents and young adults is critical to healthy functioning. Sport participation is frequently assumed to promote positive developmental outcomes; however, the moral implications of participation in combative sports such as wrestling remain debated. Wrestling differs from many team and individual sports due to its physically dominant and one-on-one competitive structure, raising questions regarding how involvement may relate to moral identity, moral disengagement, and social behavior. The purpose of this exploratory quantitative study was to examine associations among moral identity, moral disengagement, and prosocial and antisocial behavior in adolescent and young adult athletes who participate exclusively in individual sports. Other variables of interest included years of participation in wrestling, gender, and sport type (combat or non-combat) whether they predicted variation in moral and behavioral constructs. Fifty-three participants included adolescent and young adult individual sport athletes between the ages of 12 and 22. Correlational and multivariate analyses were conducted to examine relationships among variables. Moral disengagement demonstrated a significant positive association with antisocial behavior in sport. Moral identity was not significantly related to antisocial behavior and showed only a small, non-significant association with prosocial behavior. Years of participation in wrestling and sport type did not significantly predict moral identity, moral disengagement, or social behavior. Gender differences emerged for moral disengagement and antisocial behavior, with female wrestlers reporting lower levels of both. These findings suggest that cognitive mechanisms used to justify behavior may play a more central role in antisocial conduct than moral self-concept alone. The results contribute to ongoing discussions regarding the developmental implications of participation in combat sports and provide groundwork for future research examining moral processes and behavior in individual sport contexts.

title: Parent perspectives on the potential use of smart inhalers for asthma management in children: a qualitative interview study.
abstract: Achieving adequate adherence to preventer medication remains a challenge in the management of paediatric asthma. A minimum of 75% adherence is recommended to achieve adequate clinical control, however actual adherence rates are often lower and are influenced by the unpredictability of family life and competing demands. Smart inhalers aim to support adherence to preventer medications by monitoring use and providing medication reminders, as well as tracking reliever use. This study explored the perceptions of parents of children aged 5-9 years with recent uncontrolled asthma regarding the potential usefulness of smart inhalers to manage their children's asthma, and perceived barriers and facilitators to their use. Semi-structured interviews were conducted via Zoom with parents residing in New South Wales, Australia. Interviews explored parents' perspectives about barriers to asthma management, awareness and perceived need for smart inhalers, desired features and functionalities, attitudes towards data sharing, perceived support requirements and cost considerations. Data were analysed using a hybrid inductive analysis approach. Ten parents participated (children aged 5-8); none had previously used a smart inhaler to manage their child's asthma. Overall attitudes toward smart inhalers were positive. Four primary themes were identified: perceived benefits of smart inhalers, including access to reliable medication data to share with healthcare providers; barriers to adoption, including concerns about technology difficulties; cost considerations with affordability influencing the likelihood of uptake; and implementation needs including the need for support for initial set up. Parents generally viewed smart inhalers as a promising tool for managing childhood asthma. Study findings suggest that successful implementation will require consideration of cost, ease of use, and adequate support for use.

title: Evaluating Postoperative Antimicrobial Prophylaxis Practices: A Pediatric Surgery Quality Collaborative Effort.
abstract: Inappropriate postoperative antibiotic exposure in children contributes to avoidable adverse events without reducing surgical site infections (SSI), yet postoperative surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis (SAP) use varies widely across children's hospitals and determinants of effective stewardship remain unclear. This study evaluated variation in prophylaxis use and outcomes, identified drivers of inappropriate use, and characterized strategies employed by high-performing institutions to promote antimicrobial stewardship. We conducted a mixed-methods project across 30 National Surgical Quality Improvement Program-Pediatric (NSQIP-Ped) hospitals participating in the Pediatric Surgery Quality Collaborative. Phase 1 analyzed NSQIP-Ped SAP Semiannual Reports to quantify variation in postoperative prophylaxis use (>24 hours), SSI rates, and identify outliers. Phase 2 surveyed surgical quality improvement (QI) leaders and Antimicrobial Stewardship Program representatives regarding data use, QI initiatives, and interdisciplinary collaboration. Phase 3 involved semi-structured interviews with high- and low-performing hospitals, guided by the Theoretical Domains Framework, to examine organizational, behavioral, and cultural determinants of stewardship performance and to identify barriers, facilitators, and effective practices. Postoperative SAP use >24 hours varied 11.8-fold among hospitals (1.5-23.7%; case-mix-adjusted rate ratios: 0.32-3.78) with no correlation between prolonged prophylaxis and SSI rates (r = -0.086, p = 0.652). High- and low-performing hospitals reported similar perceived barriers. Determinants of success included supportive culture, standardized protocols, shared accountability, and multidisciplinary collaboration led by engaged QI champions. Substantial variation in postoperative antibiotic use exists without SSI benefit. High-performing centers achieved expected SSI rates without prolonged prophylaxis, highlighting an opportunity for targeted knowledge-sharing to strengthen pediatric surgical antimicrobial stewardship.

title: Exploring infant safe sleep practices and sleep arrangement motivations in a South African sample.
abstract: Sudden unexpected infant death remains a significant public health concern, with South Africa reporting among the highest incidence globally. However, little is known about infant sleep practices, motivations for sleep arrangements, or adherence to safe sleep recommendations within this context. This study explored caregiver and child characteristics associated with potential sleep-related risk, and caregiver motivations underlying infant sleep arrangements, among South African caregivers. A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 201 caregivers of infants. Prevalence of adherence to American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines was determined. A safe sleep composite score, derived from items of the Brief Infant Sleep Questionnaire-Revised, classified caregivers into low-, moderate-, and high-adherence groups. Bivariate associations between demographic characteristics and low-adherence group membership were examined using chi-square tests, with hierarchical multiple regression to identify predictors of adherence to guidelines. Prevalence of motivations for sleep arrangements were determined and compared across demographic characteristics. Bed-sharing and non-supine sleeping was common. title: Bullying, Cooperation, and Social Manipulation: Relations with Social Power in Adolescence
abstract: Bullying is frequently used alongside prosocial strategies to achieve social dominance while minimizing social costs. However, the nature of this combination remains unclear, as prosocial strategies have been variously conceptualized as altruistic, mutually beneficial, or competitive and self-serving. The present study investigates whether bullying is associated with cooperative prosocial strategies—marked by collaboration, reciprocity, and mutual benefit—or with socially manipulative strategies characterized by ingratiation, insincerity, and manipulation for self-serving ends. A sample of 477 secondary school students (54.5% boys, 45.5% girls; Mage = 15.49) completed peer nomination measures assessing bullying, cooperative prosocial strategies and social manipulation, and three facets of social power: social dominance (dominance and popularity), peer affection (likeability and number of friendships), and dating popularity. Results indicated that bullying was significantly associated with socially manipulative strategies but not with cooperative strategies. Cooperative strategies were most strongly linked to cooperative relationships with an expectation of mutual benefit (peer affection, dating popularity), whereas social manipulation had the strongest association with social dominance, a more competitive form of social power. Boys’ direct bullying, and indirect bullying combined with high levels of social manipulation, were positively related to social dominance. These findings underscore the importance of distinguishing cooperative prosocial strategies from social manipulation and suggest that socially acceptable cooperative behaviors may serve as viable alternatives to bullying within anti-bullying interventions.

title: In search of prosociality in rodents: A scoping review.
abstract: Studying prosociality in rodents can provide insight into brain mechanisms potentially related to neurodevelopmental disorders known to impact social behaviors (e.g., autism spectrum disorder). While many studies have been published suggesting promising models, current knowledge remains scattered, including potential factors mediating prosocial behaviors in rodents. Prosocial behavior is characterized by an action done to benefit another or promote their well-being. The goal of this scoping review is to characterize current findings regarding prosocial paradigms in rodents, highlight current gaps in reporting, and identify factors shown to be important in mediating prosocial responses in rodents. Five databases were consulted in search of relevant studies published between 2000 and 2020 (APA PsycInfo, Embase, MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science). An update using a semi-supervised machine learning approach (ASReview) was then conducted to collect studies from 2021-2023. In total, 80 articles were included. Findings were the following: (1) Three categories of prosocial paradigm were extracted: cooperation, helping, and sharing tasks, (2) Rodents showed the ability to perform prosocial actions in all three categories, (3) Significant gaps in reported methodologies (e.g., failure to report animals' characteristics, housing conditions, and/or experimental protocol) and mediating factors (e.g., sex, strain, housing, food restriction) were found, and (4) Behaviors are determinant when investigating prosociality in rodents, however many studies omitted to include such analyses. Together these results inform future studies on the impact of mediating factors and the importance of behavioral analyses on the expression of prosocial behaviors in rodents.

title: Social capital, cooperation, and the role of schools: evidence from an experiment with children
abstract: Abstract The experimental literature in economics largely acknowledges the role of social capital in social payoff enhancing behavior and/or voluntary provision of public goods. However, social capital is often measured using different proxies that, in principle, may have different impacts on contributions. In this article, we unpack social capital in three dimensions (i.e., school, family, and friends) and we analyze which dimension matters for contributions in economic experiments. We collect data from an ultimatum game, a trust game, and a public good game carried out with children in primary and secondary schools in Sicily, Italy. To measure social capital, we also collect detailed information on social attitudes related to different contexts. We find that, as expected, social capital matters for contributions. More interestingly, we find that the only component that affects contributions is social capital at school. Our findings shed a light on how the school environment may be extremely important for the formation of social capital, especially when this is linked to behavior within the same environment.

title: Training for cognitive agility
abstract: This phenomenological qualitative study is an investigation of U.S. military-affiliated educators who teach senior military leaders people skills, such as self-awareness, emotional management, prosocial skills, and creativity, with the aim of enhancing military mission effectiveness by strengthening a leader's cognitive agility. The purpose of this study was to understand how educators experience the challenges and opportunities of translating people skills into practice, equipping leaders to manage stress, uncertainty, and decision-making demands in complex environments. Consequently, this study also addresses how educators ensure people skills are taught and implemented (or transferred) successfully within the target learner's organization. Traditionally, military executive training focused on operational or managerial grooming. Very few programs focused on people skills. However, the U.S. Armed Services are increasingly focusing on providing training to mitigate negative indicators among personnel and challenges in recruitment and retention. Thus, the focus of this study was on educators who provide these training protocols. The target audience for these protocols comprises senior military leaders. These veteran leaders present some educational challenges for instructors at the outset of training, such as overcoming a stigma associated with "softness," which might be perceived as weak in military culture, compounded by an "expertise" learner bias. The research addressed how these educators develop their lesson plans to meet the needs of military learners, the obstacles they face, and the strategies they employ to foster a productive learning environment. Findings from this study will contribute to a deeper understanding of the unique pedagogical challenges and opportunities in government-based military education programs.
