title: Revitalizing the Culture of Pinnapigas in Tubo, Abra
abstract: Pinnapigas is a custom in which the residents of Tubo, Abra participate in a shared traditional meal. The study explores the cultural importance of pinnapigas in Tubo, Abra, identifies the factors contributing to the decline of pinnapigas, and proposes interventions for their preservation. The study employed a qualitative design, conducting interviews with residents of Tubo, Abra, using purposive sampling. The researcher finds out that pinnapigas symbolize values of generosity, interconnectedness among the community, and cultural identity. However, some factors impacted the decline of such practice, such as modernization, urbanization, changing lifestyles, technological advancements, and migration. The study concludes that the active involvement of younger generations through workshops and community dialogues is significant for preserving pinnapigas, assuring their continuity for future generations. In addition, this research is relevant to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of SDG 2: Zero Hunger in promoting traditional food practices through preservation of knowledge in cultural food resources, also the SDG 4 on Quality Education in handing down knowledge and skills that provide educational opportunities for the younger generation to learn about their heritage.

title: Unmasking Superficial Charm: Defining and Measuring it in the Social Context
abstract: This thesis explores the behavioural, contextual, and perceptual foundations of superficial charm, presenting a reconceptualisation of charm as a multidimensional, context-sensitive, and socially regulated construct. Across six empirical studies, it develops and tests the Superficial Charm Measure (SCM), which differentiates superficial charm into three core behavioural dimensions: Performed Social Fluency, Strategic and Instrumental, and Genuine Prosocial. These factors reflect distinct, but interacting, modes of charm expression, ranging from emotionally sincere and affiliative behaviours to those that are strategically motivated and manipulative. Using a multi-method approach—including qualitative thematic analysis, psychometric scale development, facial expression analysis, and interaction paradigms—this research examines how charm is broadcast, perceived, and interpreted across interpersonal contexts. Study 1 used qualitative interviews to identify behavioural traits associated with both charm and superficial charm, forming the foundation for item development. Studies 2 and 3 refined and tested the three-factor structure of the SCM. Studies 4 through 6 examined contextual moderators of charm perception, including social power, sex, observer bias, and the distinction between third-party observers and direct recipients. Key findings demonstrate that sex, social power, and target familiarity with the charmer significantly influence how charm is interpreted. The findings position superficial charm as a norm-driven, strategic, and co-constructed interpersonal behaviour. It is a measurable, socially embedded phenomenon that lies at the intersection of authenticity, influence and deception. Additionally, the development of the candidate measure, the SCM, contributes a novel tool to clinical, forensic, organisational, and interpersonal contexts, as well as the study of social influence, impression management, and social perception—although further validation is required.

title: Variable Phenotypic Manifestations of Novel Compound Heterozygous CRPPA Variants in Two Iranian Siblings With Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophy.
abstract: Dystroglycanopathies are a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of muscular dystrophies caused by impaired glycosylation of α-dystroglycan, with variants in multiple genes, including CRPPA, which is associated with a broad spectrum ranging from congenital muscular dystrophy to limb-girdle muscular dystrophy. The proband underwent whole exome sequencing, while Sanger sequencing was used for segregation analysis and oligonucleotide array-CGH was performed to confirm the copy number variant. We report two siblings harboring an identical novel compound heterozygous CRPPA genotype, comprising a novel c.267G>C missense variant and a deletion encompassing exons 9-10. Despite sharing the same genotype, the siblings showed marked phenotypic variability. The female sibling developed childhood-onset disease with proximal weakness involving both the upper and lower limbs, whereas the male sibling presented with late-onset disease and weakness confined to the proximal lower limbs, accompanied by markedly discordant serum creatine kinase levels (1193 vs. 460 U/L). These findings expand the mutational and clinical spectrum of CRPPA-related dystroglycanopathy, highlight marked intrafamilial phenotypic variability, and emphasize the importance of integrated single-nucleotide and copy number variant analysis in the genetic diagnosis of neuromuscular disorders.

title: Anthropomorphizing Used Products: The Role of Generalized Gratitude During Disposal Decisions
abstract: ABSTRACT Gratitude has been widely studied in various contexts, with generalized gratitude representing a prototypical form that involves being thankful for all types of gifts in life, rather than specific benefits conferred by others. While research has explored gratitude's influence on interpersonal behaviors and consumer decision‐making, the impact of generalized gratitude on product disposal decisions remains largely unexamined. To address this gap, we propose that generalized gratitude positively affects the likelihood of retaining used products during disposal decisions (Studies 1a, 1b, and 1c). We further hypothesize that anthropomorphic tendency and emotional attachment act as serial mediators in this relationship (Studies 2a and 2b). Additionally, we suggest that this effect will be attenuated when donation becomes a salient option (Study 3), when product value is high (Study 4), or when the justification for disposal is strong (Study 5). This study offers several unique theoretical contributions. We first advance the literature on gratitude by exploring its prototypical structure and examining the nature of generalized gratitude through the lens of anthropomorphic tendencies. Furthermore, we extend the understanding of disposal behavior by jointly considering a comprehensive set of influential factors, including instant emotion, product state, and situational stimuli. Our findings provide valuable insights for governments and companies, offering a better understanding of how to communicate with consumers through generalized‐gratitude‐related appeals during product disposal decisions.

title: An Eye-Tracking Study on Six Early Social-Emotional Abilities in Children Aged 1 to 3 Years
abstract: BACKGROUND: The experimental evaluation of young children's socio-emotional abilities is limited by the lack of existing specific measures to assess this population and by the relative difficulty for researchers to adapt measures designed for the general population. METHODS: This study examined six early social-emotional abilities in 86 typically developing children aged 1 to 3 years using an eye-tracking-based experimental paradigm that combined visual preference tasks adapted from pre-existing infant studies. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study is to obtain developmental norms in six early social-emotional abilities in typical children aged 1 to 3 years that would be promising for an understanding of disorders of mental development. These developmental standards are essential to enable comparative assessments with children with atypical development, such as children with Profound Intellectual and Multiple Disabilities (PIMD). RESULTS: The participants had greater spontaneous visual preferences for biological (vs. non-biological) motion, socially salient (vs. non-social) stimuli, the eye (vs. mouth) area of emotional expressions, angry (vs. happy) faces, and objects of joint attention (vs. non-looked-at ones). Interestingly, although the prosocial (vs. antisocial) scene of the socio-moral task was preferred, both the helper and hinderer characters were equally gazed at. Finally, correlational analyses revealed that performance was neither related to participants' age nor to each other (dismissing the hypothesis of a common underpinning process). CONCLUSION: Our revised experimental paradigm is possible in infants aged 1 to 3 years and thus provides additional scientific proof on the direct assessment of these six socio-emotional abilities in this population.

title: The Bystander Typology Scale: Development and Validation of a Workplace Bullying Bystander Response Measure
abstract: ABSTRACT Bystanders, organizational members who witness but are not directly involved in workplace bullying, are increasingly viewed as integral in addressing bullying. However, empirical evidence about how bystanders act and why is limited, having been hampered by the lack of a validated measure to capture bystander behavior. Drawing from previous typologies and extending a sensemaking model of bystanders, we theorize that there are four main classes of bystander behavior and that individual and organizational factors influence which of these is enacted when workplace bullying is witnessed. We develop the Bystander Typology Scale (BTS) to test our propositions, validating the new measure across three studies ( N Study 1a = 588; N Study 1b = 361; N Study 1c = 251), which show that the BTS captures four distinctive bystander behaviors: active constructive (e.g., confronting the perpetrator), passive constructive (e.g., offering emotional support), passive destructive (e.g., ignoring the situation), and active destructive (e.g., revictimization). Our main study ( N Study 2 = 374) shows that self‐efficacy, dark triad traits, and organizational conflict cultures influence bystander behavior in distinctive ways. Our research contributes to a greater understanding of how bystanders behave when witnessing bullying and why, alongside a tool for researchers to examine bullying bystanders systemically and for practitioners to evaluate interventions.

title: Linda’s Cars versus Dominik’s Dolls: How Do Pedagogical Educators in Training React to Children’s Violations of Gender Stereotypes?
abstract: The gender stereotypes adults hold can influence whether they approve or disapprove of behavior shown by children, depending on whether this behavior is in line with stereotypes. Adults report negative evaluations toward children whose behavior does not adhere to gender stereotypes, particularly toward feminine boys. Whether pedagogical educators in training show negative reactions toward children who violate gender stereotypes has not been examined. We investigate this question by firstly assessing what gender stereotypes adults hold about children in Germany. In Study 1, we assessed descriptive, prescriptive, and proscriptive gender stereotypes identified by adults for children in German society. Stereotypes gathered from this first study were used to construct four vignettes of stereotypical and nonstereotypical boys and girls in order to examine how pedagogical educators in training (N = 414) evaluated these children in Study 2. We investigated ratings of one of these vignettes (2 × 2 between-participants design) regarding liking, perceived competence, creativity, self-esteem, prosocial behavior, as well as internalizing and externalizing problems. A series of ANOVAs revealed that girls displaying masculine behavior received advantageous ratings on competence, creativity, and self-esteem, while boys showing femininity were perceived as the most prosocial. More than gender nonconformity, masculinity and femininity strongly related to externalizing and internalizing problems, respectively. We review how our results in Germany differ from the literature originating in the USA, as we did not find backlash for feminine boys. Possible bias against femininity and toward masculinity within society and cultural and sampling factors is discussed.

title: Beyond ad hominem attacks: A typology of the discursive tactics used when objecting to news commentary on social media
abstract: Social media platforms increasingly serve as the primary place where people participate in public conversations about news. In these conversations, ad hominem attacks are quite common. Such ad hominem attacks might be influenced by underlying cognitive or affective goals, such as to discredit a purveyor of falsified evidence or to signal social distance from a hateful provocateur. They may also be driven by a simple operative goal: to stop what was said. When ad hominem attacks are used to stop the comments of another person, we refer to it as a discursive objection tactic. In this paper, we explore the prevalence of ad hominem attacks and characteristics of other discursive tactics used by people when objecting to online news commentary. First, we conducted a content analysis of more than 6,500 comment replies to trending news videos on YouTube and Twitter and identified seven distinct discursive objection tactics. Second, we examined the frequency of each tactic's occurrence from the 6,500 comment replies, as well as from a second sample of 2,004 replies. Our findings confirm that while ad hominem attacks are the most common discursive tactic used to object to news commentary, people also deploy a diversity of other discursive objection tactics. The resulting typology offers a comprehensive account of grassroots efforts which utilize deterrent speech, nonaccommodative communication and prosocial strategies.

title: Self-organizing social systems: boundaries of cooperation and coordination
abstract: Networked problem solving underlies the formative dynamics of a variety of complex systems. In this setting it is important to consider not just what network ties exist, but how ties change over time, and the influence this has on the behavior and exchange facilitated by these interactions. Ranging from cellular communication to human organization, collectives engage in goal-oriented behavior and adapt to maximize their rewards. When considering a network tie between two problem solvers, optimal group-level outcomes often depend on two overarching concepts: cooperation and coordination. The first two projects of this dissertation use stylized models of networked problem solvers to demonstrate how preferential interaction (i.e., adapting network ties to maximize individual rewards) can lead to distinct system dynamics. In one setting, preferential interaction is shown to harm cooperative prosocial behaviors, while in the other it promotes coordination and robustness. The first agent-based model demonstrates the conditions under which spiteful behavior could emerge. Spite is a behavior that harms both the actor and recipient, and therefore its emergence is evolutionarily counterintuitive. The model demonstrates that if agents are able to interact preferentially, spiteful behavior can gain a relative advantage and become the norm in a population. A second agent-based model examines the formation of signaling conventions under preferential interaction. This is the first model to demonstrate agents' use of a novel form of signaling, where communicating partners failed to reach a consensus on the meaning of each signal. Instead, agents solved the signaling problem by using the network structure to ensure two distinct types of complementary signaling strategies interacted. Finally, the third project reports on an online survey and experiment conducted on an online labor market platform. This project examines the psychological willingness of freelancers to cooperate in temporary teams, and how our results can inform platform design aimed at strengthening the social ties between freelancers. Our results suggest that our freelance participants display traits that are more consistent with belonging to a shared, coherent group than would be expected given existing theory. Overall, the chapters of this dissertation consider self-organization in game theoretic and real-world settings, and show how emergent behaviors are influenced type of relational links that form. --Author's abstract

title: Adoption Strategies and Workarounds in the Evolution of Information Infrastructures Integrating Health and Social Care Providers in Scotland: Multimethod Qualitative Case Study of the Key Information Summary.
abstract: care records are digital technologies designed to support information sharing and care coordination across fragmented health and social care systems. However, adoption and use of these technologies can vary across diverse health and care settings, with users using workarounds and other strategies to meet their specific information needs. In Scotland, the Key Information Summary (KIS) has been in use for over 13 years, sharing key patient information from general practitioners (GPs) with other health and care providers for future care planning. Using the KIS as a case study, this study examines how various adoption strategies and workarounds have shaped the evolution of regional information infrastructures integrating health and social care in Scotland over time. This multimethod qualitative study examined the various contextual factors influencing adoption and use of the KIS across diverse health and care settings. Data collection included interviews with KIS users from health and care settings, implementers, and vendors; documentary analysis of user guides, websites, reports, and policies; and observation of multidisciplinary team meetings and technology use. Data analysis involved a hybrid approach. The technology-people-organization-macroenvironment framework was applied to code interview, documentary, and observational data, followed by an inductive analysis informed by science and technology studies theories of information infrastructures, domestication, and workarounds to examine strategies and workarounds for adapting the KIS to local contexts and evolving needs. Data comprised 54 qualitative interviews, 59 documents, 2 websites, and 20 hours of observational field notes collected between April 2024 and March 2025. Findings indicate that adoption of the KIS varied across settings and over time due to misalignment between system design, evolving expectations of integrated care, and national initiatives during the COVID-19 pandemic that repurposed its use. Professional roles and associated information needs shaped differing expectations of what constituted useful information, generating tensions between users who relied on the KIS and GPs responsible for maintaining it. Formal workarounds enabled the extension of the health care-centric infrastructure into nonclinical settings to facilitate information sharing with GPs and, in some cases, supported clinician access to the KIS during system outages. Across settings, informal user-driven repair practices enabled diverse professionals to adopt and realign the KIS with its intended use. This study demonstrates how regional information infrastructures integrating health and care evolve incrementally as they become embedded within local routines, practices, and existing systems. Adoption was shaped by professional roles, information needs, and users' capabilities, with formal workarounds extending infrastructures into new settings and informal, user-driven repair practices supporting ongoing use and maintenance. Policymakers and vendors must recognize that workarounds and user-driven repair practices are central to infrastructural growth and sustainability, and understanding these strategies can inform future technology development and innovation.

title: Mindfulness training reduces the preference for proenvironmental outcomes.
abstract: Theoretical accounts posit that mindfulness promotes proenvironmental behavior. While this claim is supported by correlational findings, past intervention studies provided no evidence that enhancing mindfulness increases self-report measures of proenvironmental behavior. Here, we tested whether a 31-day mindfulness intervention strengthens preferences for proenvironmental outcomes with decision tasks involving real conflict between participants' selfish interests and beneficial consequences for the environment. To unravel the psychological mechanisms underlying the impact of mindfulness on proenvironmental behavior, we assessed the impact of mindfulness training on prosociality and future orientation. Contrary to our hypotheses, the mindfulness intervention reduced instead of increased preferences for proenvironmental and prosocial outcomes, whereas no effects were observed on future orientation. Baseline preferences for proenvironmental and prosocial outcomes (and the intervention effects on them) were correlated, providing empirical evidence for a link between proenvironmental behavior and prosociality. Together, the current data suggest that the relationship between mindfulness and proenvironmental behavior as well as prosociality may be more complicated than assumed in the literature.

title: Functionally Useful but Strategically Unreliable: Exploring Crowdfunding Adoption and Campaign Development by Institutions
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper explores how professional fundraisers in cultural and charitable institutions adopt and experience crowdfunding as a new digital fundraising tool. While crowdfunding has existed for over two decades, institutional uptake in Europe remains limited compared to individual use. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Technology–Organisation–Environment (TOE) framework, this study examines fundraisers' perceptions of crowdfunding's usefulness, ease of use and organisational support. Based on 38 semi‐structured interviews with Dutch fundraisers and crowdfunding experts, the findings reveal that crowdfunding is valued for its capacity to attract new audiences, enhance visibility and test innovative ideas. Yet, there is a clear tension in institutional crowdfunding: although crowdfunding is authorised at the organisational level, limited organisational support and shared responsibility leave its implementation dependent on the effort, visibility, networks and skills of individual fundraisers, preventing it from becoming fully embedded in organisational routines. Crowdfunding relies heavily on informal practices, which some fundraisers perceive as unprofessional and/or uncomfortable. The study contributes to the literature on philanthropic marketing by demonstrating that the implementation of crowdfunding depends not only on its technological affordances but also on the organisational and environmental conditions that shape fundraisers' engagement. Implications are offered for practitioners seeking to integrate crowdfunding into broader fundraising strategies.

title: The effect of experiences of fairness on honest behavior: a behavioral and neural study.
abstract: Prior studies have investigated the relationship between fairness and honesty. However, the differences in the focus of these studies have rendered cross-comparisons between them challenging and of limited value. Thus, this study explored how fairness impacts honest decision-making, focusing specifically on the effect of individuals' experiences of fairness on their honest behavior. Experiment 1 explored the influence of different experiences of fairness on honest behavior in an altruistic context. In Experiment 2, we measured event-related potentials to further demonstrate the brain mechanisms of these experiences on altruistic dishonest behavior. In Experiment 1, we found that the reaction time for dishonest behavior was shorter for individuals who had positive unfairness experiences with high altruistic objects compared to low altruistic objects. Individuals who had negative unfairness experiences had shorter reaction times when engaging in dishonest behaviors for the sake of high altruistic objects compared to those with equitable experiences. In Experiment 2, in which there was an opportunity to lie for a highly altruistic object, those with fair experiences had greater N2 volatility and smaller P3 volatility than those with positive unfairness experiences. These findings highlight the value of integrating moral psychology and behavioral economics. Discriminant validity across fairness experiences can help illuminate the different motivations behind moral decisions.

title: Kindness in Children and Adolescents: Conceptualization and Interventions
abstract: Kindness, from the perspective of positive psychology and character strengths, is a virtue that supports others’ emotional and practical needs, strengthens relationships, and fosters a positive, inclusive social environment. Kindness can be defined as characterized by a set of behaviors, attitudes, and dispositions rooted in care, empathy, respect, and prosocial motivation. Kindness is a multidimensional, prosocial construct that developmentally evolves, shaped by cognitive development, personal and interpersonal factors, and social contexts. As individuals mature across childhood and adolescence, their understanding and expression of kindness become more complex, reflecting growing social and relational awareness and competency.

title: Bystander Behaviour and Associated Factors in Cyberbullying among Indian Adolescents and Young Adults
abstract: Background Cyberbullying has emerged as a major public health and psychological concern in the digital era. Its harmful consequences extend beyond victims and perpetrators, affecting bystanders who witness online aggression. The way bystanders respond whether by helping victims, remaining passive, or supporting the bullying can significantly influence the impact and continuation of cyberbullying. Understanding the factors that shape these responses is therefore essential for developing effective prevention and intervention strategies. Objective This study examined the different forms of bystander behaviour in cyberbullying and explored the demographic, psychological, and family-related factors associated with these behaviours among secondary school students. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 578 secondary school students in Indore, India. Participants were selected through simple random sampling from four randomly chosen schools. Data were collected using an online questionnaire that assessed demographic characteristics, cyberbullying experiences, bystander behaviour, attitudes toward cyberbullying, parental attachment, and self-esteem. Standardized instruments, including the Revised Inventory of Parent Attachment and the Revised Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, were used to measure parental attachment and self-esteem. Results The findings indicated that helping or defending victims was the most frequently reported bystander response (34.6%), followed by ignoring cyberbullying incidents (28.0%) and participating in cyberbullying (26.3%). Students who had personally experienced cyberbullying or had witnessed it affecting friends or family members were more likely to support victims, particularly when they reported stronger parental attachment. In contrast, participants who were only aware of cyberbullying involving the general public were more likely to remain passive. Those who admitted engaging in bullying behaviour and expressed favourable attitudes toward cyberbullying were more likely to join or reinforce online bullying. Conclusion The study highlights that bystander behaviour in cyberbullying is shaped by both personal experiences and psychosocial factors, particularly parental attachment. Strengthening positive family relationships and encouraging supportive bystander responses may help reduce passive observation and active participation in cyberbullying. Future research should continue to examine the mechanisms influencing bystander decisions to support the development of effective prevention and intervention programmes.

title: Leveraging social media for youth engagement in HIV prevention: evaluation of the Y-FIT GH open-call campaign in Ghana.
abstract: Adolescents and young adults (AYA) in Ghana continue to experience barriers to HIV prevention, including stigma, limited awareness of HIV self-testing and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and insufficient access to AYA-friendly prevention services. This descriptive process evaluation examined how a 2-month, multi-platform communication strategy supported participation in the Youth-Friendly Innovation Tools for HIV Prevention in Ghana national open call for creative HIV self-testing and oral and long-acting PrEP advocacy ideas. The strategy combined paid Facebook advertising, LinkedIn dissemination, and peer-to-peer WhatsApp sharing. Data included platform analytics, dissemination records, application data, and participant-reported awareness sources. Facebook recorded 55 437 impressions and an estimated reach of 48 596 users; LinkedIn generated 650 impressions, 209 engagements, and 171 link clicks. WhatsApp was the dominant self-reported awareness pathway, although individual-level WhatsApp reach, engagement, and conversion could not be measured. A total of 103 eligible AYA submitted written, visual, and audio-visual entries. The findings indicate that organizers can combine broad-reach promotion with peer and institutional networks, mobile-first materials, multiple submission formats, and prospective source tracking. Because exposures overlapped and channel metrics were not equivalent, the study does not establish causal platform superiority. Multi-channel communication can support participatory HIV prevention while requiring offline and assisted options for AYA with limited digital access.

title: Understanding Empathy Through Lived Experiences of Autistic Women
abstract: Background: Research on empathy in autism has historically emphasized deficits in social cognition and relied on male-dominant samples (Lemos et al., 2026; Loomes et al., 2017; Song et al., 2019). Consequently, less is known about how autistic women experience empathy, particularly in relation to masking, gendered social expectations, and communication differences. Objective: This exploratory qualitative study examined how autistic women describe and make sense of their lived experiences of empathy, investigated contextual factors that shape how empathy is experienced and expressed, and explored what can be learned from autistic women to advance the understanding of empathy. Methods: A participatory co-design (PCD) approach was used to center autistic perspectives throughout the study (Gomez, Kyza, & Mancevice, 2018). Three autistic women collaborated with the researcher to co-design semi-structured interview questions (Cooper, Kumarendran, & Barona, 2024; Nicolaidis et al., 2011). Nine autistic women participated in the interviews, which were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis with iterative inductive and deductive coding. Results: Empathy was conceptualized as multidimensional, involving emotional identification, affective experience, perspective taking, and prosocial behavior. Participants described intense emotional experiences, difficulty identifying specific emotions, and a disconnect between internal emotional experiences and outward expression. Participants also described masking and camouflaging as effortful processes that were influenced by gendered expectations. Experiences of being misunderstood contributed to feelings of isolation and reluctance to communicate emotional needs, whereas supportive environments facilitated understanding. Participants described reciprocal communication difficulties with both autistic and non-autistic individuals, gendered expectations and masking or camouflaging, which shaped experiences of empathy and emotional expression. Conclusions: The findings challenge previous conceptualizations of empathy in autistic women and emphasize the importance of distinguishing between expressing, and having empathy recognized by others. Centering autistic women's lived experiences provides a more nuanced understanding of empathy as heterogeneous, contextually shaped, and relational. Future research should continue incorporating autistic perspectives and examine how gender, masking, and communication influence the expression and recognition of empathy. *Language Statement: The language ‘autistic’ is used when referring to individuals on the autism spectrum to respect and utilize the language preferred by the majority of autistic individuals (Taboas et al., 2023).

title: 24-hour movement behaviour composition associated with desired social-emotional functioning in the early years.
abstract: Movement behaviours (sleep, sedentary behaviour, and physical activity) influence numerous health outcomes in children, including their social-emotional development. The optimal 24-hour movement behaviour composition for positive social-emotional development is unknown. The purpose of this study was to determine the movement behaviour composition across the 24-hour day associated with desired social-emotional functioning in the early years. This cross-sectional analysis included 560 children aged 1.2-2.9 years and 1,500 children aged 3.0-4.9 years from the Sleep and Activity Database (SADEY) for the Early Years study. Sedentary behaviour (SED), light physical activity (LPA), and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) were measured using ActiGraph accelerometers. Sleep duration was assessed using parent reports. Children social-emotional functioning was measured using the five domains of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), a widely used screening instrument of children's behaviours, emotions, and relationships across five domains (emotional problems, conduct problems, hyperactivity, peer problems, and prosocial behaviour). Compositional data analyses were used to estimate the 24-hour movement behaviour compositions associated with optimal scores for each of the SDQ domain z-scores and all five domains combined (the Goldilocks day). The movement behaviour composition was significantly associated with all five SDQ domains (all p < .01). For 1-2-year-olds, the Goldilocks day consisted of 12 h 12 min of sleep, 4 h 36 min of SED, 5 h 48 min of LPA, and 1h 24 min of MVPA. For 3-4-year-olds, it consisted of 12 h 08 min of sleep, 4 h 27 min of SED, 5 h 49 min of LPA, and 1 h 36 min of MVPA. The duration of total physical activity and MVPA associated with more favourable social-emotional functioning exceeded the minimum levels specified in the current 24-hour Movement Guidelines. These findings should not be interpreted as behavioural recommendations but rather as movement behaviour patterns associated with more favourable outcomes within this study population.

title: Roles of empathy in altruistic cooperation in adults with and without autism spectrum disorder.
abstract: Altruistic cooperation (AC) is essential in human social interactions. Previous studies have investigated AC-related behavior in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), revealing that there is considerable individual variability in the behavior. However, this issue is still largely unexplored especially in the adult population. To investigate individual differences in AC-related behavior, we conducted the resource allocation task (RAT) and modified version of the ultimatum game (mUG) among adults with and without ASD. The study employed a cross-sectional design, involving 27 adults with ASD (mean age 29.1 ± 4.3 years; three females) and 27 adults with typical development (TD) (mean age 25.8 ± 6.7 years; two females), who completed the RAT and mUG tasks. Beyond clinical characteristics, we assessed three primary psychological metrics: the interpersonal reactivity index (IRI), Barratt impulsiveness scale, and the behavioral inhibition and activation systems. No significant differences were observed in the proportions of participants with high AC when assessed by RAT (p = 0.15) and mUG (p = 0.59) between the TD and ASD groups. Participants with high AC from the RAT demonstrated higher perspective-taking scores on the IRI than those with low AC within both the TD (p = 0.04) and ASD groups (p = 0.03). In the TD group, high AC individuals also scored higher on the IRI's fantasy subscale as per the mUG (p = 0.03); however, this trend was not present in the ASD group. The present findings indicate that empathy plays an important role in individual differences in AC-related behavior among adults with and without ASD, although the role could be different depending on the types of AC-related behavior between TD and ASD populations.

title: Prosocial Motives to Serve in Rural Areas: An Exploratory Study Among Health Profession Education Students
abstract: Healthcare professionals are presumed to have highly prosocial motives that drive them to serve their communities. Contrary to this presumption, in many countries, including Indonesia, reluctance to serve in remote and rural areas appears to persist among healthcare professionals. This phenomenological study aimed to explore in depth health professionals’ perceptions of prosocial motives, their significance, and the factors that contribute to them, particularly in relation to their decisions to serve in rural areas. Using maximum variation sampling, this study recruited 17 health profession education (HPE) students as well as five related professionals (rural health workers and a social psychologist) as key informants. Data were obtained via two focus group discussions and seven in-depth interview sessions. Interview transcripts were semi-manually extracted using Prosa.ai© – an artificial intelligence (AI)-based software – and analysed using Braun and Clarke’s six steps of thematic analysis. Four themes emerged: (a) conceptualisation of prosocial motives among HPE students and professionals regarding rural area service; (b) the significance of prosocial motives for rural health professionals; (c) hindering factors of prosocial motives in serving the rural areas; and (d) cultivating factors of prosocial motives in serving the rural areas. Prosocial motives may represent an important factor in retaining rural health workers, despite the challenges of practising in these areas. To achieve a sustainable distribution of rural health workers, collaboration between government and educational institutions is needed to develop rural health policies and curricula that cultivate prosocial motives among HPE students.

title: Price Transparency and Patient Engagement: Social Messaging Matters
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To examine the effects of price transparency and prosocial messaging on price-protected consumers' health care choices as a potential cost-saving strategy to manage rising US health care expenditures. STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study. Participants were recruited to complete a basic questionnaire via Amazon's Mechanical Turk program. Participants' selections were subsequently collected and analyzed. METHODS: Participants (N = 567) selected a sleep study provider from 5 options, with manipulations including financial responsibility, provision of price information, and a prosocial message encouraging high-value options. RESULTS: Price transparency increased the selection of lower-cost options among participants who were solely responsible for paying for their own health care expenses. For participants whose insurance paid for health care expenses, both price transparency and prosocial messaging were necessary to choose lower-cost options. CONCLUSIONS: The study highlights the importance of considering both financial and social factors in patient engagement initiatives, suggesting that a combination of price transparency and prosocial messaging can influence health care choices and potentially contribute to cost-saving strategies in the US health care system.

title: Social Media Use and Digital Professionalism in Nursing Practice: Cross-Sectional Questionnaire Study.
abstract: The rapid growth of social media has transformed communication, with more than 5.66 billion users worldwide in 2025 who spent an average of 141 minutes daily on platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube, and TikTok. Nurses frequently use social media to exchange work-related information, communicate with others, and relieve stress. While social media can support professional development, excessive or inappropriate use at work may compromise patient care. Despite widespread use, research on nurses' demographic factors and actual workplace social media behaviors remains limited. The aim of the study was to determine how nurses use social media at work and how their demographic characteristics (eg, gender, age, and number of years working in health care) are related to the use of social media at work. This study used a quantitative, descriptive, exploratory, and nonexperimental empirical research design. Data were collected via a survey administered to a convenience sample of 132 nurses. The sample comprised of 98 women (74.2%) and 34 men (25.8%). The questionnaire consisted of 17 statements related to social media use in the workplace. A statistical significance level of Nurses used Facebook the most and spent between 45 minutes and 1 hour per day on social media. Study participants reported that they primarily used social media for communication with colleagues and acquiring new knowledge. They also used social media for its technical functions, such as file sharing. Nevertheless, a substantial number of nurses reported using social media during working hours, and many had experienced creating an uncomfortable situation after declining social media interactions with patients or colleagues. This study highlights the important topic of social media use at work by nurses. The study found that nurses frequently used social media, primarily for professional communication and knowledge acquisition. While most demonstrated positive use patterns, the findings indicate that social media use during work may pose potential challenges to professionalism. These results highlight the need for clear guidelines and training to ensure that nurses use social media responsibly, maintaining both professional boundaries and personal integrity. Encouraging mindful and regulated use can enhance the benefits of social media while minimizing risks in the health care setting.

title: The relevance of top-down self-regulation for children's and adolescents' developmental outcomes.
abstract: A popular topic in developmental science is self-regulation, an aspect of functioning viewed as contributing to optimal development. Of particular theoretical importance is top-down (frontal cortically based) self-regulation (TDSR). This article briefly reviews recent research on TDSR's relation to four areas of development: maladjustment, social competence, prosocial development, and academic development. Recent studies on the topic often involve sophisticated methods and designs; moreover, several relevant meta-analyses have been published in the recent past. In general, a higher level of TDSR has been associated with better adjustment, social competence, prosociality, and success in the school setting. Limitations in the research and extant meta-analyses are briefly noted.

title: Satuwakaf Indonesia App in the Eye of Indonesian Youth: Comparing Millennials and Gen Z Preferences
abstract: Background: Indonesia's demographic bonus provides an opportunity to expand digital waqf participation among Millennials and Generation Z through the Satuwakaf Indonesia application. Therefore, there are urgencies to analyse the behavior and preferences of Digital Waqf among Indonesian Youth. Method: This study employed a quantitative approach within a sequential explanatory mixed-method design. Data from 428 respondents were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), Multi-Group Analysis (PLS-SEM MGA), and robustness testing. Results: Attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioral control, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, outcome satisfaction, expectation, and altruism significantly influenced digital waqf intention, whereas process satisfaction did not significantly affect expectation. Altruism also strengthened the relationships between TPB constructs and behavioral intention. Multi-group analysis indicated that the structural model was generally consistent across Millennials and Generation Z, with a significant difference only in the relationship between outcome satisfaction and expectation. Conclusion: Integrating TPB, ETAM, and altruism provides a comprehensive framework for explaining digital waqf adoption and offers practical guidance for improving digital waqf platforms and increasing youth participation.

title: Positive youth development and mental health in Latine adolescents experiencing discrimination: A mixed-methods study.
abstract: The role of Positive Youth Development (PYD) and prosocial involvement in buffering the impact of racial-ethnic discrimination among Latine adolescents remains understudied. To examine whether PYD and community-level opportunities and rewards for prosocial involvement moderate the association between discrimination and depressive symptoms and suicidality in Latine adolescents through a mixed methods approach. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Latine adolescents (N = 110), assessing racial-ethnic discrimination (Everyday Discrimination Scale [EDS]), depressive symptoms and suicidality (Mood and Feelings Questionnaire [MFQ]), PYD (PYD Short Form), and community-level opportunities and rewards for prosocial involvement (Communities That Care scales). Linear and logistic regression models examined predictors of depressive symptoms and suicidality. Moderation was tested with interaction terms. Semi-structured interviews were completed with a nested sample of adolescents and caregivers (N = 18 dyads). A thematic analysis of interviews with a focus on the role of PYD was conducted. EDS scores were associated with higher MFQ scores and suicidality. PYD factors and community-level opportunities and rewards for prosocial involvement were associated with lower MFQ scores and suicidality. These trends were generally consistent in adjusted regressions. None of the PYD factors, nor community-level opportunities and rewards for prosocial involvement, moderated these relationships. Qualitative findings identified youth-described processes consistent with PYD that appeared to support coping in the context of discrimination. PYD factors and community-level opportunities and rewards for prosocial involvement are associated with improved mental health among Latine adolescents but may not be sufficient to buffer the harmful effects of racial-ethnic discrimination.

title: EKONOMİDE YARDIMSEVERLİK: BİR İNCELEME
abstract: This article delves into charitable behavior through the lens of economics, exploring how altruism and generosity intersect with economic decision-making. It traces the historical evolution of charity, from its early roots in religious and ethical traditions in ancient civilizations, such as Egypt and Greece, to its institutionalization in modern philanthropic practices during the Industrial Revolution. The analysis draws heavily on behavioral economics, focusing on key theories like warm glow-giving, reciprocal altruism, and social preferences, which challenge traditional economic models of rational self-interest. By incorporating psychological factors, such as emotional satisfaction and social recognition, these theories offer a more comprehensive understanding of why individuals engage in charitable acts. The article also investigates the impact of framing effects and social norms on donation behavior, revealing how the presentation of philanthropic causes and social contexts shape giving decisions. Finally, it examines the role of tax incentives in promoting charitable contributions and how government policies can be designed to encourage more effective and widespread generosity, contributing to broader social welfare objectives.

title: Social comparison shapes the evolution of cooperation in structured populations
abstract: Human cooperation unfolds in social environments where individuals influence each other through payoff-based learning and social comparison, the tendency to evaluate fitness relative to others. However, it is still unclear how social comparison and population structure jointly shape cooperation. Here, we incorporate social comparison theory into evolutionary dynamics on structured populations, letting fitness depend on individual and neighbour payoffs weighted by a comparison parameter. Under weak selection, we derive conditions favoring cooperation and find that the proposed comparison nonlinearly reshapes the critical benefit-to-cost ratio. Even one individual applying this protocol can affect the population, especially in heterogeneous networks. When comparison tendencies vary, the full distribution, not just the mean, determines evolutionary outcomes. Using a swarm-intelligence-based framework across typical and empirical networks, we identify cooperation-maximizing patterns: optimal states exhibit heterogeneous comparison tendencies, yet collectively align toward assimilative development. These results provide a basis for designing social incentives that harness comparison to promote collective cooperation in human groups.

title: Designing History-Based Educational Games to Improve Cognitive Empathy in Children with ASD: A Pilot Study
abstract: Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) face significant challenges in Theory of Mind (ToM), particularly in understanding others' perspectives. While serious games have shown potential, most existing interventions focus on basic emotion recognition without engaging narrative contexts. Objective: This pilot study aims to design a history-based serious game, "Tarumanegara Adventure," and evaluate its preliminary effectiveness in improving cognitive empathy among children with high-functioning ASD. Using a mixed-methods case study approach with a one-group pretest - post-test design, six students with ASD (aged 8-15) participated in a 2-week intervention. The game integrates historical narratives as a logical scaffold with explicit emotion scaffolding and moral decision-making mechanics. Data were analyzed using the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test and triangulated with behavioral observations. Quantitative results showed a significant increase in cognitive empathy scores (p = 0.0312) with a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 3.19). However, triangulation revealed a "knowing-doing gap," in which higher cognitive scores did not correlate significantly with spontaneous prosocial behavior (ρ = -0.36). Conclusion: The history-based narrative approach effectively enhances cognitive knowledge of empathy by providing a structured context. However, bridging the gap between cognitive understanding and spontaneous behavioral application remains a critical challenge for future game design.

title: Cost-benefits analysis of joint actions; children and adults estimate the potential effort of acting together.
abstract: Every day we engage in activities that require collaboration and assistance from others. Social interactions with children are distinct because they frequently result in partners contributing different amounts of effort. This study investigates the decision-making processes underpinning joint actions; specifically, whether children and adults estimate they will have to invest different amounts of effort when engaging in joint tasks compared to doing the same task by themselves. In 4 Experiments, children and adults estimated the weight of objects when they anticipated that they would be lifted alone and when they thought they would have help. Children and adults estimated the weight of 3 clear baskets carrying different weights (light, medium, and heavy). The estimated weight of objects varied for adults and children depending on whether they thought they would lift alone or together. Children reliably perceived objects as lighter when they expected help from their parent compared to lifting them alone or with the help of a sibling. Parents, in turn, estimated objects would be heavier when they were helping their child. Overall, results suggest that we analyze the costs and benefits of helping another person and the social bond we have with them before engaging in joint actions.

title: From duty to dialogue: the evolution of professional trust across two generations in Mauritius
abstract: Background: Medical professionalism is a core component of health professions education (HPE), yet prevailing frameworks have largely been developed from provider perspectives and within Western contexts. The perspectives of patients and communities, particularly in African and multicultural settings, remain underrepresented. In addition, little is known about how generational differences shape expectations of professional conduct in healthcare. Methods: This qualitative narrative inquiry investigated perceptions of medical professionalism among 32 participants in Mauritius, including 16 from Generation Z and 16 from Generation Y. Data were collected through individual narrative interviews guided by six flexible prompts: (1) an instance when a healthcare worker exceeded expectations; (2) a moment of uncertainty or discomfort in a healthcare environment; (3) a time they observed or experienced unprofessional behaviour; (4) what stood out most to them; (5) their interpretation of what it means to be a professional doctor; and (6) how their personal values influenced their expectations of doctors. The prompts served as flexible narrative guides rather than a rigid interview schedule. Participants were encouraged to develop their narratives freely and in their own sequence, with follow-up probes used where appropriate to clarify meanings, elicit further detail, and deepen their accounts. This approach provided consistency in the broad areas explored across participants while remaining aligned with narrative inquiry principles by privileging participants' experiential accounts and meaning-making. Interviews were conducted in English, French, or Mauritian Creole and transcribed verbatim. Ethical approval was secured from the National Ethics Committee of the Republic of Mauritius (Protocol MHC/CT/NETH/2025/A V2). Results: Nine themes were identified. Six themes: Humanised Care, Communication and Information Sharing, Respect and Dignity, Ethical Integrity and Trustworthiness, Accountability and Consequences, and Clinical Competence were strongly represented across both generations, forming a shared relational moral core consistent with Ubuntu-informed understandings of professionalism. Three themes showed significant generational differences. References to consent, autonomy, cultural sensitivity, and partnership-based communication were prominent in most Generation Z interviews. In contrast, Generation Y participants emphasised professional duty, vocation, moral responsibility, and stewardship more frequently. The most distinctive finding was the prominence of Duty, Vocation, and Moral Obligation among Generation Y participants (9/16) and their complete absence from Generation Z narratives (0/16). These differences suggest contrasting mechanisms through which professional trust is established and maintained. Discussion: These differences seem to reflect varying social environments rather than a decline in professional values. Generation Y grew up within more hierarchical healthcare relationships, where trust was primarily established through professional authority and moral obligation. In contrast, Generation Z has been raised in a digitally connected, rights-conscious environment that emphasises the active construction of trust through dialogue, transparency, and participation. Thus, medical professionalism in Mauritius can be understood as a fundamentally relational moral practice rooted in dignity, empathy, integrity, accountability, and competence, which serve as core values that resonate across generations, even as the preferred methods for fostering professional trust vary by cohort. Rather than signalling a shift from relationality to autonomy, these findings indicate a transition between different forms of relational professionalism. This study offers community-based insights to inform the development of culturally responsive and generationally sensitive professionalism curricula, particularly in African and other multicultural healthcare contexts.

title: Why are younger-age adults reluctant to give blood? A reflexive thematic analysis of non-donors in the United Kingdom
abstract: The present study explored the psychosocial factors influencing blood donation behaviour among younger-age adults classified as non-donors in the United Kingdom. Six participants (aged 18–35) with no history of blood donation were recruited via opportunity sampling. Semi-structured interviews were conducted and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis to identify key patterns in participant narratives related to donation behaviour. Two overarching themes were identified. Barriers to blood donation included four sub-themes: (i) socially constructed misconceptions of eligibility and need, (ii) embodied discomfort and perceived invasiveness of the donation process, (iii) disengagement and deferred responsibility in blood donation, and (iv) perceived absence and inaccessibility of blood donation campaigns. Facilitators of blood donation included three sub-themes: (i) promoting blood donation by addressing diverse reward preferences, (ii) the importance of procedural clarity in reducing uncertainty, and (iii) increasing motivation to donate blood through cues to act. Tailored public health strategies must address adult non-donors’ psychological and informational barriers, including misconceptions, procedural uncertainty, and anxiety about physical reactions. Interventions should pair targeted communication with accessible, accurate information and frame donation as both socially beneficial and personally rewarding.

title: Sex-Specific Associations of Small, Vulnerable Newborns With Mental Capital in Early School-Aged Children.
abstract: Although mental capital is increasingly recognised as a foundation for children's later well-being, its perinatal determinants remain unclear because traditional classifications such as preterm birth and small for gestational age (SGA) capture only partial and overlapping aspects of vulnerability. Using the integrated small vulnerable newborn (SVN) framework with mutually exclusive categories, we aimed to assess associations between SVN categories and mental capital at ages 6-7 years by sex. We analysed data from six waves of the Adachi Child Health Impact of Living Difficulty (A-CHILD) study, a population-based repeated cross-sectional survey of first-grade students in Adachi City, Tokyo, conducted between 2015 and 2024 (n = 20,928). Caregivers provided gestational week and birthweight from the Maternal and Child Health Handbook, and children were classified into SVN categories (term non-SGA, term SGA, preterm non-SGA, preterm SGA). Mental capital, including behavioural problems, prosocial behaviour, and resilience, was assessed using the parent-reported Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire and Children's Resilience and Coping Scale. Multivariable regression models were fitted, stratified by biological sex. Among the 20,928 children, 3402 (16.3%) were term SGA, 1093 (5.2%) were preterm non-SGA, and 227 (1.1%) were preterm SGA. Compared with term non-SGA, term SGA was associated with higher total difficulties scores among girls (standardised β 0.11, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.05, 0.17) but not among boys (β 0.03, 95% CI -0.03, 0.09). Term SGA girls also showed lower resilience (β -0.07, 95% CI -0.12, -0.01). In contrast, preterm non-SGA boys had higher total difficulties scores (β 0.13, 95% CI 0.04, 0.21). There was no evidence that any SVN category was associated with prosocial behaviour in either sex. Term SGA tended to be associated with behavioural problems and lower resilience among girls, whereas preterm non-SGA tended to be associated with behavioural problems among boys.

title: Early social-cognitive development as a dynamic developmental system—a lifeworld approach
abstract: Based on developmental systems and dynamic systems theories, we propose the lifeworld approach-a conceptual framework for research and a hypothesis concerning early social-cognitive development. As a framework, the lifeworld approach recognizes the social embeddedness of development and shifts the focus away from individual developmental outcomes toward the reciprocal interplay of processes within and between individuals that co-constitutes early social-cognitive development. As a hypothesis, the lifeworld approach proposes that the changing developmental system-spanning the different individuals as their subsystems-strives toward attractor states through regulation at the behavioral level, which results in both the emergence and further differentiation of developmental attainments. The lifeworld approach-as a framework and a hypothesis, including key methodological approaches to test it-is exemplified by research on infants' self-awareness, prosocial behavior and social learning. Equipped with, first, a conceptual framework grounded in a modern view on development and, second, a growing suite of methodological approaches, developmental science can advance by analyzing the mutually influential relations between intra-individual and interactional processes in order to identify key mechanisms underlying early social-cognitive development.

title: Communicating global income rank
abstract: People in high-income countries underestimate their affluence relative to the global population, potentially limiting their will- ingness to donate to charity. We test whether a rank-based nudge (RBN) informing individuals how their post-tax income ranks globally increases charitable donations. Further, because people have been shown to shift their reference point for who should give to charity based on their current income, we inves- tigate whether donations can be boosted by asking how much people with different income ranks should give to charity (in- junctive distribution task, IDT) before administering the RBN. Participants (N = 1,217) were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: control, RBN, IDT, or IDT+RBN. Those in the RBN conditions donated significantly more and reduced over- estimation of others' income across all percentiles of the global income distribution. However, the addition of the IDT did not further increase donations. These findings suggest that RBNs effectively boost generosity by correcting misperceptions of relative affluence.

title: Encouraging Ethical and Practical Local Government Managers: How the ICMA Code of Ethics Promotes Servant Leadership
abstract: This study empirically examined the association between the adoption of ethical codes and servant leadership in local government organizations. Analyzing survey data from the International City/County Management Association (ICMA) from 2012-2018, along with the U.S. Census Bureau’s Community Engagement and Volunteering Supplement (CEVS) to the 2021 Current Population Survey (CPS), this study explored how the associations between adoption, scope, and enforcement mechanism of ethical codes impacted seven categories of servant leadership: relationships with elected officials, policy collaboration, information exchange, innovation, performance effectiveness, service delivery, and public/community engagement. This study also explored the relationship between ethics training and these seven dimensions of servant leadership. Although evidence suggests that compliance-based ethics infrastructure such as ethical code adoption and a broadly-applying ethical code scope is associated with servant leadership, integrity-based ethics initiatives, namely a robust, continuous ethics training program, shows the strongest association with servant leadership outcomes in local government.

title: Measuring dispositional empathy in South African children.
abstract: Empathy is a key factor to examine in development, because of its predictive associations with both aggression and successful prosocial behaviour. However, established measures of empathy for Low-to-Middle Income Countries, including South Africa, are lacking. In children, parent-report measures are key. However, a local study examining empathy and aggression (Malcolm-Smith We contrasted internal consistency reliability of a simplified version of the GEM (SGEM; The parent-report version of the QCAE performed well as a measure of child dispositional cognitive and affective empathy, with good reliability (overall α = 0.90 vs. SGEM α = .63), and confirmatory factor analysis supporting the two-factor structure. The SGEM's reliability and failure to correlate with QCAE indicated poor psychometric performance. title: Mental health problems in a large representative sample of children and adolescents: Prevalence, associations with problematic substance use and psychometric properties of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire.
abstract: Mental health problems are already widespread in childhood and adolescence. The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) is an internationally widely used instrument for assessing mental health problems and prosocial behavior in children and adolescents. Particularly, the Total Difficulties score (TDS) from the SDQ (calculated from the sum of all problem scales) is considered a good estimator for mental health problems. Heretofore, there are relatively few estimates for mental health problems based on representative samples that rely on self-assessments by children and adolescents. Although SDQ is frequently used internationally, the findings regarding its psychometric properties are inconsistent. So far, there are no results available from representative samples on the relationships between the TDS and various forms of problematic substance use. A representative sample of 4001 12-17-year-olds from Germany was examined using the SDQ with regard to mental health problems and established standardized instruments for problematic use of alcohol, cigarettes, and cannabis. We calculated relative frequencies, reliability coefficients (Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega), correlations, binary logistic regressions, and linear regression analyses. Furthermore, we conducted confirmatory factor analyses. Based on the TDS, 9.6% (95% confidence interval: 8.7%-10.5%) of the representative sample reported severe mental health problems. We observed reliability values for the five SDQ scales between 0.44 (peer problems) and 0.70 (emotional problems), as well as 0.74 and 0.75 for the TDS. In the different confirmatory factor analyses, no model showed a completely satisfactory fit to the data. In bivariate and multivariable analyses, consistent statistically significant associations were found between mental health problems (TDS) and problematic cigarette use and problematic cannabis use, whereas findings for problematic alcohol use were mixed. According to our results, a substantial proportion of German children and adolescents are affected by severe mental health problems, and problematic substance use is a possible source of this.

title: The Evolved Nest in Childhood: Relation to Adult Well-being and Social Capital Across Cultures
abstract: Abstract Evolved nests are species-specific developmental systems that support biological, psychological, and social needs. The human evolved nest includes practices such as responsive care, self-directed play, and extensive affectionate touch. Previous studies have linked childhood experience of these practices to both child and adult well-being. Here we assessed whether recall of evolved nest experiences during childhood (age 0–18) was related to three dimensions of adult well-being and social capital (personal well-being, social relationships, and general prosociality) in three countries (USA, UK, Japan). Recalled evolved nest experience was positively associated with multiple measures under each dimension across cultures after controlling for demographic factors ( n = 1,401). In contrast, it was not found to be associated with incentivised measures of prosociality (elicited via a series of economic games) in any country. Exploratory factor analyses revealed that experiences of evolved nest practices clustered together under two common factors in each country: positive and negative experiences. These factors were independently associated with multiple indicators of adult well-being and social capital in each country, and these associations were generally stronger for positive (vs. negative) experiences. Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that childhood experience of the evolved nest has long-term benefits for individual and societal well-being regardless of cultural differences.

title: Associations between dysfunctional parental discipline and parent-reported mental health outcomes in preschoolers: a cross-sectional study.
abstract: This study explored the association between parental discipline and mental health in a sample of 21,366 Chinese preschool children (mean age = 4.82 ± 0.89 years; 51.77% boys, 48.23% girls). Parenting practices were measured as overall parenting scores, laxness, overreactivity, and verbosity, and children's mental health was assessed by the official simplified Chinese version of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ). Both outcomes were dichotomized using validated cut-offs for Chinese preschoolers, and odds ratios are reported as the odds of meeting these cut-off definitions (Total Difficulties Score > 14; adequate Prosocial Behavior Score ≥ 6). The results indicated that higher parenting scores (for total difficulties: AOR = 4.03; 95% CI: 3.64-4.46; for prosocial behavior: AOR = 0.48; 95% CI: 0.45-0.51), particularly in laxness (for total difficulties: AOR = 1.28; 95% CI: 1.23-1.34; for prosocial behavior: AOR = 0.88; 95% CI: 0.85-0.91) and overreactivity (for total difficulties: AOR = 1.83; 95% CI: 1.76-1.90; for prosocial behavior: AOR = 0.66; 95% CI: 0.64-0.68), were associated with higher odds of a Total Difficulties Score > 14 (i.e., risk of mental health difficulties) and lower odds of an adequate Prosocial Behavior Score (≥ 6), while verbosity (for total difficulties: AOR = 0.80; 95% CI: 0.77-0.84; for prosocial behavior: AOR = 1.23; 95% CI: 1.19-1.27) was associated with lower odds of a Total Difficulties Score > 14 and higher odds of an adequate Prosocial Behavior Score (≥ 6). Subgroup analyses suggested potential effect modification by education level and child age, but most interaction effects were not significant after multiple comparison correction. The findings emphasize the need for balanced parenting and interventions targeting both discipline and parental well-being to enhance children's mental health.

title: Depth or Breadth? The Impacts of Monetary Incentives on the Direction of Free Knowledge Contributions
abstract: In this study, we examine how changes in monetary incentives offered to online consultants on e-consultation platforms shape the direction of their free knowledge contributions across specialized and non-specialized domains. We use the sudden suspension and subsequent resumption of the Fenda platform as two exogenous shocks to the monetary incentives these online consultants receive, and implement a difference-in-differences estimation. Our study shows that monetary incentives shift the direction of online consultants’ free knowledge contributions. Rather than delving deeper into their specialized domains and engaging with even unpopular topics, they tend to broaden their contributions across a broader array of non-specialized domains. The findings enrich the literature on knowledge management and provide valuable guidance for managers of e-consultation platforms.

title: Kapwa Ko, Kaibigan Ko: Unmasking Friendship Between Children with Autism and Non-Neurodivergent Children through the Lens of Kapwa Theory
abstract: More than just a social activity, friendship becomes a child’s earliest avenue for belongingness, where they learn connection, reciprocity, and empathy. However, for children diagnosed with autism, previous studies have indicated that social deficits often serve as barriers to establishing friendships, particularly with non-neurodivergent peers. This qualitative phenomenological study explored how Children with Autism (CWA) and Non-Neurodivergent (NND) children define friendship, how friendships are established and maintained between cross-neurotypes, and how these children relate to and treat their friends. Data were gathered through dyadic interviews of seven (7) pairs of friends, consisting of one CWA and one NND child. The data were interpreted through the lens of Kapwa Theory, a fundamental concept in Sikolohiyang Pilipino. Reflexive Thematic Analysis revealed that among the friendship pairs, friendship was defined as a source of emotional security, the embodiment of kindness, a lasting connection, and a personification of the concept of friendship. Friendships were formed through nurturing bonds via mutual engagement and bridging connections through social scaffolding. These friendships were maintained by cultivating a sense of sustained togetherness and upholding social harmony. Participants treated their friends by displaying emotional attunement, providing instrumental support, and responding with reciprocal generosity. These findings demonstrate that CWA and NND children are capable of both reciprocating and accommodating within friendships, evidenced by their expressions of pakikisama, pakikiramdam, and the value of kapwa. Moreover, these findings challenge the long-standing notions that friendships between CWA and NNDs are inherently one-sided and prone to misunderstanding and conflict.

title: Timmy’s Trip to Planet Earth: The Long-Term Effects of a Social and Emotional Education Program for Preschool Children
abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Social and Emotional Education (SEE) interventions during early childhood have shown considerable promise in enhancing children's emotion understanding, social competence, and behavioural adjustments. However, few studies have examined their long-term impact, especially across the preschool-to-primary school transition. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a manualized SEE program, Timmy's Trip to Planet Earth, in promoting emotional, behavioural, and social functioning over time. METHODS: = 44). The program combined teacher training, classroom-based lessons, home activities, and teachers' ongoing implementation support. The effectiveness of the program was measured via the Test of Emotion Comprehension (TEC), the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), and the Social Competence and Behavior Evaluation (SCBE-30). RESULTS: Significant Time × Group interactions were observed for the TEC External and Mental components, indicating greater improvements in emotion recognition and mental state understanding in the intervention group. The SDQ revealed significant reductions in conduct problems and increased prosocial behaviours. In the SCBE-30, a significant interaction effect was found for social competence, with the intervention group showing greater improvement over time compared to the control group. CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that SEE programs can produce meaningful and lasting improvements in children's emotional and social skills across key educational transitions. Teacher training and family involvement likely played a critical role in supporting the program's sustained impact.

title: Navigating the Unknown: Understanding the Impact of Mentorship for First-Generation Students in Stem
abstract: First-generation students often encounter systemic barriers and inequities in academic pursuits related to science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM). Many institutions implement mentoring programs to mitigate these challenges; however, the effectiveness of STEM mentoring relationships for first-generation college students has been underexplored in the empirical literature. The current study centers the voices of first-generation college students to explore how mentors and institutions can better support their success through STEM mentoring relationships. In addition, this study examines how mentors’ generational status informs how they approach mentoring relationships with first-generation mentees. Participants included mentors and first-generation mentees in STEM research mentoring relationships who completed one-hour in-depth interviews. The sample consisted of 22 first-generation mentees, 16 first-generation mentors, and 19 continuing generation mentors, spanning 15 states and capturing a diverse range of perspectives. A map of all participating states is presented in the Appendix, Figure 1. Thematic analysis revealed challenges first-generation mentees encountered in STEM research, including navigating implicit rules and expectations. It also highlighted mentoring behaviors that supported a first-generation mentee’s growth, such as intentionally sharing social capital. These findings provide valuable insight into how institutions and mentors can create tailored support to better serve their first-generation college students in STEM research.

title: Effective altruism, technoscience and the making of philanthropic value
abstract: A recent philanthropic movement with advocates among high-profile tech entrepreneurs and philosophers, effective altruism (EA) has been widely disparaged for its flawed moral philosophy and conservative political implications. As philanthropic practice, however, it has been seldom studied. In this paper, we argue that claims to technoscientific expertise are central to how EA actors understand, legitimize, and take part in the production of philanthropic value. We analyze their practices of categorization, ranking and measurement as well as underlying technoscientific imaginaries and moral views through comparing three areas of EA intervention: neglected tropical diseases, cultured meat, and AI safety. We show how EA involves various and contested ambitions to direct knowledge production and redraw the boundaries of expert communities, shedding light on the centrality of technoscience in philanthropists' worldmaking ambitions.
